Highly placed sources told The Indian Express that within hours of the Left announcing its withdrawal of support on Tuesday, the government had conveyed to the IAEA that it was willing to finalise this draft. The next morning, India's representative on the IAEA Board of Governors put in a formal request to circulate this draft to all the other members of the Board. Once it was circulated to the Board members, the document became public and was put on the MEA website.

As senior cabinet minister Kapil Sibal put it, once the Left parties had withdrawn their support, the government was under no constraint to wait any further and therefore decided that it was time to request IAEA to circulate the draft.

The safeguards agreement underlines all the basic principles that have been mentioned in India's separation plan as also the 123 Agreement, namely the assurance of uninterrupted fuel supply for the lifetime of safeguarded reactors, reprocessing and enrichment rights, the need to maintain a strategic reserve of fuel and the right to take corrective action in the event of disruption of fuel supplies.

Heading: 3 months ago, Karat pledged: Deal will die, Third Front will live - Indian Express
Content:
The Indian Union Muslim League (IUML), the oldest Congress ally in the UPA and the party of the MoS for External Affairs, E Ahamed, today decided to support the Government on the nuclear deal but, at the same time, convey its apprehensions about the deal to the Congress leadership.

The decision was taken during a three-hour meeting of party leaders in Malappuram, the party's headquarters.

The IUML state president, Panakkad Syed Muhammadali Shihab Thangal, told the media that Ahamed would pass on the League's anxiety on the deal to Congress president Sonia Gandhi. "The Muslim community is worried about the deal. The IUML would ask the Congress to consider the community's concerns while going ahead with the deal," he said.

Earlier, the party had even discussed the option of withdrawing Ahamed from the Cabinet but voting in favour of the government in the event of a trust vote. Such an exercise was meant to placate a section in the party which believed that the party should oppose the deal and quit the government.

The party's national president, the late G M Banatwala, had expressed his dissent in a press release on June 25, the day he died in Mumbai. In the press note, issued after his death his secretary, Banatwala said the deal was not acceptable to the IUML. He said that Bush administration's "imperialism" should be opposed. "The Congress needs to reconsider its decision," he had said.

At today's meeting, too, the overwhelming feeling was that Ahamed should resign from the Cabinet.

The CPI(M)-lef Left Democratic Front in Kerala has made consistent inroads into the Muslim League bastion in Malabar. In the last Lok Sabha election, the party lost one of its two traditional seats and the last Assembly election threw up worse results.

Apart from the CPI(M) which has packaged itself as a Muslim-friendly party, the party of Muslim moderates has been facing tough competition from Abdul Nasser Madani's PDP and the extremist National Democratic Front.

Ahamed said he would attend the UPA meeting slated for tomorrow. "The party's concern over the deal would be conveyed to Congress leaders and other members. The feedback received from the Congress would be passed on state president Shihab Thangal who would take appropriate action," he said.

Heading: Pak paper reports how Yuvraj partied night before his duck in final - Indian Express
Content:
Three short months after hot and humid Coimbatore, it's a winter of desolation for the CPM, especially for General Secretary Prakash Karat. This is not the Karat who held forth to comrades in a stuffy, red-festooned hall at the 19th party Congress in April, about the only two means at hand to take the Revolution forward: the Third Front and Death to the N-Deal.

With both these goals appearing more distant than ever, as he comes out to face TV cameras to fume over Vienna, his two trusted and senior Politburo colleagues are in London.

Both Sitaram Yechury and Biman Bose, chairman of the Left Front in West Bengal, have gone there reportedly on pre-scheduled programmes. Their absence was noted by the Opposition Trinamool Congress.

During the Budget discussion on the home department in the West Bengal Assembly today, Saugata Roy of Trinamool rubbed it in: "Why are two of your party comrades in London during such a crucial hour? Will the Chief Minister throw some light on this?" Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee preferred to remain silent.

Benoy Konar, a central committee member of the CPM, was the only one to throw some light. He said Bose left for London yesterday to deliver a lecture on the "success of mass education" in West Bengal. He said Bose was supposed to leave a week ago but could not do so given the political drama that unfolded. Konar said that Bengalis settled abroad had invited him. "It was a pre-scheduled programme and difficult for Bose to skip," said Konar.

Bose is scheduled to be back in Kolkata July 16, two days after party cadres are set to hit the streets in West Bengal in a "massive offensive" against the nuclear deal. Yechury and Bose are also scheduled to together attend a programme, party sources said.

Whatever the speculation over their absence, one thing is clear: events have over-taken the roadmap that Karat had rolled out in Coimbatore.

In fact, so smug was the party then about having its way on the nuclear deal that the issue got only a few passing references and fewer speakers even at discussions to firm the crucial political resolution. There was no separate resolution on the deal, among the several the comrades sat down to pass.

It was all too clear and simple to the party: even sending the agreement to the IAEA Board of Governors for ratification would mean putting it on autopilot and that's where the line is. And there was no way the UPA would want to cross that and risk the government.

Akalmand ko Ishara Kaafi hai (For the intelligent, a signal is enough), Yechury had then said, amplifying the Left's confidence. Asked what the party would do if the Government went ahead, he had said: "We'll take a call when it happens."

The political resolution at the Congress had a distinct triumphal tone: "India becoming a strategic ally of the United States would be a major gain for US imperialism. The Party decided to oppose the nuclear agreement as it was the cementing factor for such an alliance. The Party and the Left decided that it would do whatever is necessary to block the agreement. Faced with the political consequences of such a confrontation with the Left, the Congress and the UPA decided not to proceed further with the operationalisation of the agreement. This is a significant step forward in the struggle to prevent the United States making India its junior partner..."

But the big fulcrum of the Coimbatore Congress was always the third alternative. The coming together of the sentinels of the three mighty canons but not necessarily Red, not even Left. "A large number of interested parties opposing communalism, fighting the anti-people content of the economic reforms, resisting the country playing itself into US hands". The dream's scaffolding, comrades were told in Coimbatore, would begin immediately, the structure would be in place in a matter of months.

The third alternative, expounded the party political resolution, will be "based on a platform of policies for which the Left, democratic and secular forces can work together. Such a platform must be based on a consistent anti-communal outlook, address the problems faced by the people and advocate pro-people economic measures; it should press for provisions for social welfare and for strengthening of the public distribution system; in defence of national sovereignty and an independent foreign policy. It cannot be a mere electoral alliance to meet current exigencies. Through joint campaigns and struggles, the third alternative will emerge based on a common programme."

And then came Mulayam Singh Yadav.

Heading: Hush-hush big deal: Blog, two websites posted text  before MEA - Indian Express
Content:
When the national selection committee dropped Yuvraj Singh from the Test squad, the ostensible reason was his form during the disastrous tour of Australia. There were indications that it also had to do with his fitness, but it now emerges that his "attitude" , too, contributed to it.

According to top officials of the BCCI, the Board has decided to take a "serious view" of the player's "nightlife."

While BCCI vice-president Rajeev Shukla said the board was not going to probe into a report from Pakistan that said that three players, including Yuvraj, partied late into the night before the Asia Cup final, an official said they were, in fact, looking into the incident.

According to Pakistani daily Jang, Yuvraj, Suresh Raina and Rohit Sharma attended a late night party at Karachi's French Beach on the eve of Night before final, Yuvraj partied till 3, says Pak daily

the Asia Cup final. The report said that the players returned to the hotels at 3 am after the party, thrown by friends in Karachi. Yuvraj, Raina and Sharma scored 0, 16 and 3 respectively in the final, all falling to spinner Ajantha Mendis.

"The Board is looking into the matter. If it is true, it will be dealt with very seriously," a top official said.

One of the national selectors also said that "it's high time Yuvraj learned a lesson the hard way," warning that his lifestyle and lack of concern for fitness would not be overlooked anymore.

The injury to his knee from Champions Trophy, 2006, has been a cause of concern for a while. When the team returned from the tour of Australia early this year, Yuvraj was called to the National Cricket Academy (NCA) for a fitness test. Physio Paul Close suggested that the player needed a break. Yuvraj managed to pass the fitness test and went on to play in the Indian Premier League (IPL) and now the back-to-back one-day tours.

Heading: On second anniversary of 7/11, a tribute to the 187 lives lived - Indian Express
Content:
Deceit and betrayal — this was how the Opposition slammed the Government for telling the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to circulate the draft safeguards agreement to its Board before the trust vote. And the Left criticised it for not showing them the text. Until about 11 am today when the UPA Government posted the text on the Ministry of External Affairs website, its stand was that this was a confidential text that couldn't be made public until the Board members have taken a call on it.

Trust the worldwide web for a reality check.

A highly read blog on nuclear non-proliferation and at least two reputed non-proliferation lobbying groups, all of them US-based and all of them opposed to the nuclear deal — for reasons exactly the opposite to those cited by the Left — had posted the "confidential" agreement on their websites at least eight to 10 hours before the MEA did so.

In fact, one of these non-proliferation groups, the Arms Control Association (ACA), had even nominated CPM General Secretary Prakash Karat as one of the nominees for the Arms Control of the Year Award for this year for putting the brakes on the Indo-US nuclear deal, though he didn't win it.

First off the blocks appears to be a blog on nuclear arms control and non-proliferation (www.armscontrolwonk.com) authored by Jeffrey Lewis, who identifies himself as Director of the Nuclear Strategy and Nonproliferation Initiative at the New America Foundation and a research affiliate with the Project on "Managing the Atom" at Harvard University.

He put the "original" document up on the blog with an announcement of having posted it at 1 am IST on Thursday, barely hours after IAEA issued an official statement late last night that they had circulated the draft to the Board members. His take on the agreement is amply clear from his post, which reads "India safeguards agreement stinks" and then does a 402-word critique of the agreement.

The Arms Control Association's website, www.armscontrol.org put up the draft agreement as a PDF document dated July 9. The document has been put up along with a covering letter of the IAEA with the agency's letterhead on it, and marked as "restricted distribution." It's numbered GOV/2008/30, and is dated July 9, 2008.

Washington DC-based ACA's Research director Wade Oboese told The Indian Express, "We put it up on our website at about 5 pm local time on July 9 (Indian Standard Time: 2.30 am, July 10). The document was made available to us after IAEA circulated it amongst the Board of Governors."

Oboese said, "When we receive a document, and it merits public attention and debate, we put it up. Confidentiality doesn't mean secrets. These documents should be debated in public so that policymakers can make wise decisions."

The 27-page draft text of the safeguards agreement, also in the same PDF format just like the original document - can also be found on the website of the Institute for Science and International Security, another Washington DC-based non-profileration lobbying group. Both these groups also have India's 123 agreement with the US on their website, which have been put earlier.

Heading: Temple tree - Indian Express
Content:
Prosecutors in an Italian court Thursday asked the key middleman in the IAF's VVIP chopper deal whether the initials 'AP' in an alleged "budget sheet" for bribes to politicians referred to Ahmed Patel, the political secretary of UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi.

The middleman, Guido Haschke, who has consistently denied bribing Indian officials or politicians, replied that he did not know who or what 'AP' stood for.

As first reported by The Indian Express, Italian prosecutors had last month produced a handwritten document they alleged was a "budget" drawn up by two middlemen — Haschke and Christian Michel — which purportedly lists initials of Indian politicians and designations of bureaucrats and IAF officers who allegedly had to be "handled" to fix the Rs 3,546 crore deal.

The alleged "budget sheet" detailed how kickbacks of 51 million euros would be divided and under the heading "POL" — Haschke has claimed this referred to Indian politicians — there is a reference to "AP" against which "3 million euro" has been listed.

Another amount of 15/16 million euros was listed against "FAM" which is said to be "Family". Haschke has claimed the note was dictated to him by British consultant Michel during one of their meetings in 2008.

On Thursday, Italian prosecutor Eugenio Fusco asked Haschke during a court hearing in Busto Arsizio near Milan whether "AP" in the note was a reference to Ahmed Patel.

In his reply, the middlemen said he did not know what AP meant when he wrote it down. Haschke also denied any bribes were paid for the contract and said that the "budget sheet" was just an imaginary note drawn up and was never acted upon.

He also said the budget sheet was merely bragging by Michel about his Indian contacts and that Haschke tried to disassociate himself from the Briton.

Strongly denying any wrongdoing in the deal, Haschke also claimed to Indian interrogators in the court that no bribes were paid for the contract and that the money he received from AgustaWestland - in excess of 24 million euros - is justified as fees for engineering consultations.

Italian prosecutors also produced another note in court Thursday - a March 2008 fax by Michel to Peter Hulett, said to be the then head of region, govt sales at AgustaWestland's India office. The fax said that among the politicians who would use the choppers once acquired by India would be UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi and her senior advisors, including Ahmed Patel.

However, Sonia is not entitled to use government helicopters. She can use VIP aircraft only when she flies with the PM, President or ministers who are officially entitled to the aircraft. This fax by the British middleman has also been shared by the Italian side with the CBI team that is in Busto Arsizio for the hearing.

Michel has been elusive and no investigative agency has been able to reach him.

Haschke, who is facing a case in Italy for being part of a conspiracy to bribe Indian officials to ensure the AW 101 chopper was picked by the IAF, faced several questions from the Indian side and denied any irregularity.

But the Indian side did not ask Haschke to explain what AP, FAM or any of the other acronyms in the note - "DS", "JS AIR", "AFA", "DG Acquisition", CVC" etc - referred to, source said.

The middleman, who was quizzed about his association with former Air Chief S P Tyagi - named as an accused in the CBI case in the deal - denied that any money had been paid to the retired Indian officer. Haschke, sources said, admitted that he was in regular touch with three cousins of Tyagi who have also been named in the case.

In response to a question from the Indian side, Haschke said he was not aware if any money was paid to S P Tyagi.

The UPA government had come under pressure in connection with the alleged kickbacks last month after The Indian Express report on the budget sheet of the middlemen. The opposition BJP had demanded the government reveal what or who "AP" and "FAM" stand for. The party also said that it wants a detailed discussion in Parliament on "alleged payments to persons close to the ruling establishment" in connection with the controversial chopper deal and has accused the government of "running away from discussions".

The discussion did not take place as the Parliament session was abruptly called off midway.

Heading: Parents get life for ‘honour killing’ - Indian Express
Content:
The 800-year-old Ta Prohm shrine in Cambodia — better known as temple of trees — will soon be restored and conserved with the help of Dehradun-based Forest Research Institute (FRI). A team, led by FRI director Dr S S Negi and senior scientist Dr Sas Biswas, will supervise the entire process of conserving and restoring the temple. Besides being as old as the world famous Angkor Wat temple, Ta Prohm is unique with massive trees winding around the structure.

Almost like a giant octopus taking the temple in its tight grip, the tree trunks and roots wind through the crevices of the structure. The unique appearance of the temple draws thousands of tourists every year.

The Cambodian authorities had approached the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) to restore the temple. Years ago, the Angkor Wat temple was successfully restored by the Archeological Survey of India. Though there was no doubt that the ASI was well-equipped to restore this temple too, the question was whether it would be able to do so without touching the trees that were more than a century old. It was at this point that the FRI was approached and a team of scientists made a reconnaissance of the site in February 2007. Subsequently, they started working on a project proposal to restore the temple, without causing any damage to the trees.

"It was of prime importance that the trees do not get disturbed in any way. We studied all aspects of the area — physiological, pathological and aesthetic. We studied the area surrounding the temple in terms of its meteorology, geomorphology and bio-diversity," said Biswas.

The FRI recorded 131 trees in its study. These trees belong to 25 species with Tetrameles, better known as Speung, being the most prominent.

The project report prepared by the FRI was approved recently at a seminar of International Co-coordinating Committee for Restoration and Conservation of Monumental Heritage Sites of the World held at Siem Reap in Cambodia.

Dr Biswas said, "We have studied the region in both micro and macro terms and on the basis of our observations we have suggested the measures for conservation. For example, the trees around the temple get waterlogged during the rains and as a result, their roots get exposed. The visitors trample upon the exposed roots. We have suggested installation of small wooden planks over such roots. Similarly, visitors climb up and sit on the tree branches. We have suggested the installation of wooden culverts. We have identified the causes of disease and decay and have also come up with solutions."

The FRI proposes to cover the exposed roots of the trees with sterilised local soil. It plans to install aesthetically suitable wooden and iron props to provide support to the leaning trees. In addition to this, there is a proposal to regulate the movement of tourists near the trees. Besides supervising and supplementing the conservation of the temple and the trees, the FRI will also develop local capacities so that Cambodian experts can undertake similar projects on their own in the future.

Heading: SC stays CBI probe against Saini - Indian Express
Content:
Delivering verdict in a case of "honour killing", a sessions court here on Friday sentenced a couple to life imprisonment for killing their 18-year-old daughter after she eloped with a boy belonging to a different community.

Additional Sessions Judge O S Jaiswal held Mohammad Munna Sardar Khan and his wife Shehnaz Khan guilty of murdering their daughter Mehnaz Khan and cutting her body into 11 pieces on July 2, 2006 for eloping and marrying a Hindu Maharashtrian boy, Vidyanand Jadhav.

The court, while sentencing them to life imprisonment, observed that it is not a "rarest of the rare case" since they cut the body into 11 pieces only after strangulating Mehnaz to death with a towel. But the judge said it was "indeed one of the inhuman acts".

Considering the moral responsibility the couple have towards their other five children, the judge showed leniency while announcing the punishment and sentenced them to the minimum punishment of life.

According to the prosecution case, on July 2, 2006, Mehnaz eloped with her childhood love Vidyanand Jadhav to Panvel where they got married. When Khan learnt about this, he along with his wife approached Mehnaz and convinced her to return home, promising that they would help her settle down in life. They also assured her that they would accept her marriage to Jadhav.

But later in the evening, on reaching the Cuffe Parade residence of the accused, Khan strangulated Mehnaz to death while her mother prevented her from escaping.

Mehnaz's body was then cut into 11 pieces and her skin peeled off so that the body could not be identified if recovered. Her nose and ears were also chopped. The body was then stuffed into a gunny bag and thrown off the Byculla bridge.

The gunny bag with the body was recovered a few days later from under the bridge. The gunny bag used nailed Khan, as it was found that it came from the grocery shop, G N Shop, he ran in the vicinity.

Police Inspector Hinduram Patil, the investigating officer in the case, said, "When the body was recovered, the face was unidentifiable and badly mutilated."

Following the "last-seen-with" theory, the police solved the case within a month.

Substantial amount of material evidence found at the spot of the crime and the circumstantial evidence helped the police build their case against Khans. The couple were also fined Rs 1,000 each.

Heading: Sanskrit from Class I: MP Govt forgets its idea - Indian Express
Content:
The Supreme Court on Friday stayed till further orders a CBI investigation ordered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court against Punjab Vigilance Bureau chief Sumedh Singh Saini and other police officials for their alleged involvement in a fake encounter case.

The case dates back to December 1991 involving alleged militant Balwant Singh Multani. Saini was then SSP, Chandigarh.

A Bench of Chief Justice K G Balakrishnan, Justices P Sathasivam and J M Panchal also issued notices to the CBI besides other respondents on a petition filed by the Punjab Government seeking an "urgent" intervention from the apex court challenging the High Court's order.

According to the petition, Multani, son of a retired IAS officer Darshan Singh Multani, had escaped from police custody on December 19, 1991. He was alleged to be one of the six proclaimed offenders (POs) who were behind the terrorist strike that took place on August 29, 1991. In the attack, Saini was seriously injured along with several security and CRPF personnel.

The HC on May 30, 2007, suo motu directed trial court to place a detailed report about all six POs, including Multani.

Following which, it passed a series of orders like setting up of a special investigating team to inquire into the

POs and issuing notice to the CBI.

Acting on an application filed by Multani's father, the HC on October 5, 2007 directed the CBI to inquire about the allegations against disappearance of his son at the behest of Saini, the application alleged.

Pursuant to which, the CBI on July 2, 2008 filed a criminal case against Saini, the then DSP (Chandigarh) Harshay Sharma and the then sub-inspectors posted at the Police Station Central, Chandigarh, Jagir Singh.

On July 4, 2008, the High Court had ordered the investigating agency to complete the investigations within four months.

Heading: SP to leave Rae Bareli, Amethi for Sonia, Rahul - Indian Express
Content:
The academic session has already begun but there is no trace of the BJP Government's ambitious idea of making Sanskrit compulsory from Class I.

The proposal forwarded by the Sanskrit Board had cleared all the stages with Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan himself referring to it from time to time.

Former education minister Laxman Singh Gaud was all for the proposal but he died in a road accident in February.

Then Dr Manmohan Upadhyay, associated with Sanskrit Bharati, a body affiliated with the RSS, was unceremoniously asked to leave as vice-chairman of the board. He left on a bitter note after a fight with senior RSS leader Makhan Singh, who is BJP general secretary (organisation).

After that, others, including the CM, have shown little interest in the idea.

Education Minister Jagannath Singh said,"It was not possible to implement the proposal because we simply do not have enough teachers." To begin with, the Government had decided to recruit one teacher each at all the 313 blocks, he added.

He is right as in the mainstream government schools, where the proposal would have been implemented, there is a massive shortage of qualified Sanskrit teachers.

A former board member told The Indian Express that several Sanskrit schools came up after the NDA regime doubled the grants for Sanskrit schools. As of today, there are more than 2,000 Sanskrit schools, with many of them being run from home.

However, all's not well with these schools. Infrastructure is not adequate and copying is rampant. In the latest instance of bungling, thousands of students could not take the examination that began late last month. While the board claimed it did not receive applications, students said they did not get admit cards despite filing application forms and sending demand drafts.

The students, who missed out, approached the High Court, which directed the board to conduct a special examination for them in August-end. Already, the main examination was behind schedule. Board secretary V S Saxena blamed the delay on lack of staff and resources.

Heading: RJD looking for deal with Left in Bihar - Indian Express
Content:
Even before formalising its future electoral alliance with the Congress in UP, the Samajwadi Party has decided not to field candidates against Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi even if their alliance does not work.

"We (the SP) will leave Rae Bareli and Amethi for Sonia and Rahul in the next elections," SP general secretary Amar Singh told The Indian Express.

Singh said the coming together of the SP and Congress was in the political interests of both the parties which were committed to countering the BSP-BJP alliance. "The convergence of SP and Congress should strengthen the coalition. We will leave Rae Bareli and Amethi even if the alliance does not materialise," he said. "This alliance will not break and will see through this Government."

Denying any other deal behind the nuclear deal in supporting the Congress-led UPA Government, he maintained,"Our party will not join the Government even after it wins the trial of strength in Parliament."

Apart from keeping its flock together, the SP is also trying to get more support for the Government. "SP supports the Government and, if need be, we will also muster support of other parties," added the SP general secretary.

Within hours of the UPA coordination committee meeting on Friday, SP chief Mulayam Singh Yadav and Amar Singh met Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. "I had told the PM before his G8 visit that we should not take any step to undermine our traditional relations with Iran. He briefed us about his deliberations at the G8 summit," Mulayam told reporters after his meeting with the PM.

Singh claimed the PM also told them that US President George Bush had not made any "untoward" demand regarding Indo-Iran relations on the sidelines of the G8 summit. "PM said he had told US Congressman Gary Ackerman that just as nuclear energy was important, gas energy was also vital. Iran-Pakistan-India gas pipeline is very much required," he said, adding the PM had assured his party that "there will be no compromise on India's security and sovereignty".

RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav spoke to Singh in the afternoon in the wake of reports of resentment within the SP ranks over supporting the Government. The SP general secretary is learnt to have assured Lalu that his party — barring two MPs, Munnawwar Hasan and Jaiprakash Rawat — remained united and had also got support from two independent MPs from UP on this issue. He is also learnt to have informed Lalu about his talks with MPs in the BSP camp.

Heading: Pressure mounts on Somnath to quit - Indian Express
Content:
While members of the Congress party continue to berate the Left parties for withdrawing support from the UPA Government, RJD chief Lalu Prasad is singing paeans for the comrades, even though he had earlier charged them of blocking the nation's progress by opposing the nuke deal.

So why is the Railway Minister suddenly showering 'love' on the Left? Lalu watchers attest that his erratic comments often mask a methodical agenda and that his warmth towards the Left parties is born out of political compulsions.

Even the communist leaders are aware of this. "Laluji knows that the odds are stacked against him in the electoral arena. He needs our help in the form of an electoral alliance in Bihar. This is the secret behind Laluji's love for us," CPI state secretary Jalaluddin Ansari told The Indian Express over the phone. However, he welcomed the RJD chief's motives and said, "it seems good sense is prevailing upon him".

In the last general election, Lalu's electoral arrangement with the CPI had broken over seat-sharing and then again in the by-election for the Bhagalpur seat; last year, Lalu had elbowed out the sitting CPI(M) candidate and fielded his own nominee, leading to BJP's victory in the Muslim-dominated constituency.

"This time, Lalu is looking for the broadest possible social alliance in Bihar. Moreover, an intelligent politician like him does not want to close the option of doing business with the Left — the third largest configuration in the country," said political analyst Saibal Gupta.

For the Congress, an acrimonious relationship with the Left is fairly appropriate, as it is their principal opponent in West Bengal and Kerala. But for Lalu, the Left, with cadre bases in various pockets of Bihar, is desperately needed at a time when RJD's support base has dwindled considerably.

Senior RJD leader and MLA Shakeel Ahmad Khan confirmed that his party was preparing for an alliance with the CPI and CPI(M) in Bihar. "The Left has always been behind us in difficult times. Laluji is only reciprocating," Khan said.

There's more to Lalu's outpourings. Once a Lalu confidant and now his bitter rival, JD(U) MP Shivanand Tiwari feels the drifting Muslim vote bank plays into Lalu's effusiveness. "Lalu's political life lies in the Muslim vote bank and he knows that it is drifting away from him. Now he wants the Left's support, so that their anti-US tirades neutralise the impact of his support for the nuclear deal," Tiwari said.

Lalu, in the past, had always projected himself as anti-US to nourish sentiments of the Muslim vote bank and his "Bush Bhagao" lathi rally in Patna is still remembered. But now that he has come out as one of the strongest proponents of the nuclear deal, he has to take some damage-control measures.

Heading: Brajesh hails IAEA safeguards agreement - Indian Express
Content:
A day after Somnath Chatterjee said as the Lok Sabha Speaker that he did not owe allegiance to any political party, the West Bengal units of the RSP and Forward Bloc (FB) on Friday also called for him to step down.

"From moral and ethical points of view, the Speaker should step down since the letter given by the Front to the President withdrawing support to the UPA lists him as a Left Front MP," said Manoj Bhattacharjee, a Central Committee member of the RSP.

Ashok Ghosh of the FB said everyone should follow his party's decision. "Whether the Speaker will step down or not is up to him, but there is a moral angle. After all, he won his seat on a Left Front ticket," Ghosh said.

The Speaker, when asked by The Indian Express to comment on Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee's statement, said she had the right to move a no-confidence motion against him. Earlier in the day, Banerjee, her party's lone voice in Parliament, had said she would personally move a no-confidence motion against the Speaker.

When pointed out that a no-confidence motion required the backing of a minimum number of members, Mamata retorted that she had many 'friends' among Members of Parliament who would support her.

"I have nothing to say. What will happen, will happen on the floor of Parliament," said Chatterjee, who is still a CPI(M) card-holder. He, however, declined to comment on the statements by the RSP and FB. "They have stated their opinion. How can I comment," he said.

Asked about the vote of confidence to be sought by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, the Trinamool chief declined to reveal her cards but alleged that the Congress and CPI(M) were still hand in glove.

"I am not for toppling the UPA Government, I am for stability," she said. "But what is going on now is just a gameplan of the Congress and CPM."

She said the biggest indication of such a gameplan was that the Speaker had not yet stepped down. "Even the Congress does not want the Speaker to step down," she added.

Heading: Jaswant faced flak from party for visiting Amar Singh house - Indian Express
Content:
Hailing the Indo-US nuclear deal, Brajesh Mishra, National Security Advisor during the NDA regime, on Friday congratulated the Government on the safeguards agreement with the IAEA.

He cautioned against re-negotiating the deal. Mishra, who held the dual positions of NSA and Principal Secretary to Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, said the draft safeguards agreement is "very satisfactory" and discounted the concerns raised by some quarters over India's military nuclear programme.

"It is as good as we could have got," he told Karan Thapar in an interview on CNBC when asked about the safeguards agreement which was unveiled on Thursday.

Heading: IAEA safeguards agreement takes care of India’s strategic interests - Indian Express
Content:
Former Union external affairs minister Jaswant Singh's visit to the residence of SP general secretary and fellow Thakur leader Amar Singh last week got senior BJP leaders like M Venkaiah Naidu, Arun Jaitley, Sushma Swaraj and V K Malhotra all worked up when the BJP's core group met here recently.

Most of the 11-member club felt Jaswant's visit had come as a "huge embarrassment to the party".

"Why did you have to go to Amar Singh's residence?" asked one of them.

Another leader sarcastically remarked that "if Mulayam Singh Yadav had to be offered the top job, why not persist with the present dispensation?" At a press conference that he had earlier addressed with L K Advani, Jaswant had accepted having "made the prime ministership offer" to Amar Singh.

Jaswant sheepishly replied that he went there only after being "invited twice" by the SP leader, to which he was asked, "why didn't you then make this fact public?"

Another leader present at the meeting said the Leader of Opposition in the Rajya Sabha then wondered "if he would have to take others' permission for going out for a drink or two".

If Jaswant's afternoon visit to the 27 Lodi Estate residence of Amar Singh triggered a political storm, it also put the BJP leaders in a spot.

Clueless party spokespersons excused themselves when asked about the visit. A leader close to Jaswant claimed "he had kept Advaniji in the loop over the visit".

A core group member, however, said this was not true. "I spoke to Advaniji and even he came to know about this visit only through media reports."

After the seemingly hostile reaction at the party core group meeting, a worried Jaswant is learnt to have asked his aides to find out if his statement "had been twisted by the media".

"Jaswantji meant that the BJP would have offered support to a UNPA dispensation only if the Congress-led Government fell in the event of Bhairon Singh Shekhawat's election as President with the UNPA support. It was not as if a coup was being planned," claimed a Jaswant supporter.

Jaswant, however, could not be reached for comment despite repeated attempts.

Heading: No PILs on inter-state water disputes: SC - Indian Express
Content:
As India debates whether the safeguards agreement with the IAEA is in the interest of the country or not, a careful reading of the text of the draft agreement reveals a number of provisions which are designed specifically to address India's strategic concerns.

Most of the contentious issues like the right to maintain strategic reserve of fuel and the provision to take corrective measures in the event of disruption of fuel supplies — which have been generating a lot of debate in the country — have been addressed in the preamble itself before being reinforced with necessary provisions in the draft agreement.

So has been the assurance that India will have access to reliable and uninterrupted fuel supplies to the safeguarded reactors.

If things go as expected from here, India should be ready to put the first of its nuclear reactors under IAEA safeguards sometime next year.

The cost of putting one nuclear facility under safeguards has been put at 1.2 million euros. The IAEA has 237 safeguards agreements in force with 162 states and spent about 100 million euros in 2006 in enforcing these agreements.

Here are the provisions in the draft agreement, which bestow a special status on India:

• Paragraph 5 says that the safeguards agreement will be implemented in a manner "designed to avoid hampering India's economic or technological development" and "not to hinder or otherwise interfere with any activities involving the use by India nuclear material, non-nuclear material, equipment, components, information or technology produced, acquired or developed by India independent of this Agreement for its own purposes". This non-hindrance clause is to ensure that India's weapons programme is completely unaffected by this agreement.

• Paragraph 52(c) has a provision for India to make a 'special report' to the IAEA in case there is a disruption of operation in any of the safeguarded facilities "on account of material violation or breach of bilateral or multilateral arrangements to which India is a party".

This reinforces the assurance of reliable and uninterrupted fuel supplies by providing for a grievance redressal mechanism in the event of a default by supplying countries.

• Paragraphs 71 to 75 recognise India's need for maintaining a strategic reserve of fuel, a provision that is absent from every other safeguards agreement that the IAEA has with other countries. India has to keep the stockpiled fuel in a sealed storage capacity and agree not to remove it without informing the IAEA.

• Paragraphs 79 to 84 deal with India's reprocessing rights, again a special provision made for this country. These paragraphs also make it clear that in case of reprocessing plants having both safeguarded as well as unsafeguarded nuclear material, IAEA "shall restrict its safeguards procedure to the area in which irradiated fuel is stored".

• Paragraph 94 provides for similar arrangements in the case of enrichment plants.

Heading: Maoists blow up railway track in Bihar - Indian Express
Content:
In a significant decision, the Supreme Court has ruled that public interest litigations (PILs) cannot be filed on inter-state water disputes. The ruling, which dismissed a petition filed against Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Y S Rajashekhar Reddy, comes as a reprieve to the politician who was accused of favouring his brother's company in awarding the mini hydropower project at the Rajolibanda Diversion Scheme (RDS) in Karnataka. The RDS was an inter-state irrigational project covering Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, which comprises of an ayacut — area served by an irrigation project — of the RDS on the river Tungabhadra (the inter-state river and a tributary of river Krishna).

Dismissing the writ petition filed by Atma Linga Reddy and few other residents of district Mehboobnagar in Andhra Pradesh, who had challenged the said river project, the bench comprising Justices C K Thakker and D K Jain asserted that no public interest litigation could be filed raising inter-state water disputes either in the High Court or the apex court. "It is clear to us that such disputes cannot be the subject matter of petition either in High Court under Article 226 or in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution," read the verdict written by Justice Thakker, who in categorical words even ruled out invoking Article 131 in such disputes. Article 131, the Court explained enables the Central or state governments to file a suit in the apex court in certain special cases.

"In our considered opinion, the founding fathers of the Constitution were aware and conscious of the sensitive nature of inter-state disputes relating to waters. They therefore provided for the machinery for adjudication of such disputes relating to waters in inter-state rivers or river valleys," continued the verdict, clearly establishing that Article 262 empowered the Parliament to enact a law providing for adjudication of any dispute or complaint with regard to use, distribution or control of waters of any inter-state river. "In our opinion, it was thought proper to deal with and decide such sensitive issues once and for all by a law made by Parliament," concluded the verdict.

Heading: India sees more tourist arrivals - Indian Express
Content:
In a series of explosive attacks that took place barely 12 hours apart in eastern Bihar on Friday, Maoist guerillas blew up a portion of the block development officer's building at Lakshmipur in Jamui district and exploded bombs twice along railway tracks, apparently undeterred by the strong presence of armed security personnel in the area.

The Maoists first targeted the track between Narganjo and Ghorparan stations under Eastern Railway around 1 am and, just after it was repaired, attacked it again at 11 am.

Insurgents also exploded a bomb on railway tracks near Ghoghi-Bariarpur village on Jamalpur-Kiul section in Munger district. Though train services were disrupted, no casualties are reported.

The attacks took place during a 24-hour bandh called by the outlawed CPI(Maoist) in the 'Jamui Banka zone'-comprising Jamui, Munger, Bhagalpur, Lakhisarai and Banka-to protest the alleged custodial torture of its 'area commander' Kamlesh alias Deepak, who was arrested on July 6.

Friday's events, of course, are certainly not the first of their kind in the state, with Maoists blowing up rail tracks, police pickets and government buildings at regular intervals here, especially since the formation of Jharkhand in 2000.

In fact, 31 of 38 Bihar districts are Naxal-infested and 19 of them, including Patna, Jamui, Munger and Bhagalpur, are under the very sensitive "A" category.

Also a matter of great concern is that the CPI(M) has, of late, started using highly sophisticated weapons in major attacks, and according to police figures, at least 2,000 trained and armed ultras — supported by large cadres right down to the village level — terrorise the region. Their use of explosives in attacking police stations and government offices (see box) over the past couple of years also enables them to carry out multiple attacks in short bursts that do not give the police enough time to respond effectively.

Police sources say that another obstacle comes in the form of the "well-knit" Naxal structure, which starts from village squads and then up the hierarchy to area, zonal, special area and regional committees until the top-level Politburo.

In addition, the Maoists' operations are given their strategic edge by military commissions, propaganda bureau, specialised guerilla and base forces.

Inspector general of police (operations) S K Bhardwaj, the man in charge of anti-Naxal operations refrained from detailing police strategies and its constraints in tackling the Naxal menace. He, however, said: "As short-term measures, the police conducts raids, long-range patrolling and search operations. The police has fortified 137 police posts." Besides, a 400-member Greyhound trained STF, 23 companies of CRPF, 16 BMP battalions, and 7,000 SAP jawans besides usual district police forces are there to tackle Maoists, he said.

Heading: AGP, BJP work on strategy to defeat Cong in Assam - Indian Express
Content:
Adverse tourist advisories seem to have no impact on the 'Incredible India'. The country has witnessed a record inflow of tourists in the first six months, according to the data issued by the Ministry.

As many as 2,660,337 tourists have arrived till June this year, registering a 11.2% increase against the previous year mark, according to the data. The foreign exchange earning has leapt by 22.2%.

Various countries including US, UK, Canada had been issuing advisories from time to time to their citizens telling them to avoid travelling to certain parts of India. Alerts were issued on various issues including Darjeeling Gorkhha strike, Gurjjar protest and Jaipur bomb blast.

This had forced the Tourism Ministry to write to the MEA to take up the matter with the Missions in the important tourist-generating countries, asking them to be fully briefed on their facts before issuing any advisory. "Only when absolutely necessary, should advisories be considered and that too, in consultation with the MEA, so that facts are adequately represented," the Tourism Ministry had said.

Heading: Meghalaya Govt reduces VAT on diesel - Indian Express
Content:
The Asom Gana Parishad (AGP) has nearly arrived at an understanding with the BJP intending to defeat the Congress by as many seats as possible in the forthcoming Lok Sabha elections in Assam.

Senior AGP leader Chandra Mohan Patowari said the regional party has held a series of meetings with leaders of various Opposition parties — including the BJP — to avoid splitting of anti-Congress and ensure the defeat of Congress.

"We are working on a strategy to defeat the Congress, and it is possible to defeat the ruling party if we can stop non-Congress votes from splitting," Patowari said.

Patowari and other senior AGP leaders, including Lok Sabha member Arun Kumar Sharma and Rajya Sabha member Birendra Prasad Baishya, have already had two rounds of discussions with Sushma Swaraj and other senior BJP leaders in New Delhi.

The AGP and the BJP had won two seats each in Assam in the 2004 Lok Sabha elections while the Congress won nine.An Independent, backed by both the AGP and the BJP, won one seat. The last time, the BJP also had backing from the Bodo tribes, which had ensured victory of the BJP candidate in Mangaldoi. The Bodo tribals, however, are now a politically divided lot with one faction supporting the Congress and the other inclined towards a possible AGP-BJP understanding.

"The Congress'claim that it will win 13 seats this time, apart from the one going to its Bodo ally, is nothing but a dream... we are determined to keep all non-Congress votes in one block," Patowari, Leader of the Opposition in the state Assembly, said.

Interestingly, the AGP, which is working on a seat-sharing formula with the BJP, is also a member of the United National People's Alliance. "We have had discussions with AUDF's Badruddin Ajmal," Patowari said. Going by the results in the 2004 elections, the AGP and BJP together have an edge over the Congress in as many as 11 seats.

Heading: MP plans to make schools tobacco-free - Indian Express
Content:
The Meghalaya Progressive Alliance (MPA) Government has reduced the Value Added Tax (VAT) on diesel by 50 paisa to counter price rise on essential commodities.

There has been widespread concern over the price rise, especially of essential commodities. Hundreds of women had recently staged a protest, demanding that steps be taken to check price rise of the essential commodities at least.

Meghalaya Food and Civil Supplies Minister J A Lyngdoh said as the state depends on road transportation for essential commodities, it was pragmatic to reduce the existing diesel price. Lyngdoh said the Government took the decision because most of the essential commodities are being ferried by trucks as the state has no rail links.

Cutting diesel price was the most practical solution, he said. The Government decided against cutting down the VAT on petroleum products as the existing cost of petrol in Meghalaya is already less than that in Assam. The Government has also directed deputy commissioners of all the seven districts to hold a review meeting every fortnight to monitor prices of all the goods.

Heading: Continuous power  for BSF on border - Indian Express
Content:
The state Government has come out with a plan to banish tobacco from both public and private schools. A team comprising three students and a teacher will keep an eye on those consuming tobacco in any form. The team, to be trained for the purpose, will keep an eye on the students, teachers, staff and visitors to the school. Teachers and staffers will escape with a monetary punishment for the first offence but the subsequent offences will be noted in their CRs.

Principal secretary (Education) M M Upadhyay told The Indian Express that he had asked the district education officers to select a couple of schools in every district headquarter and a school each in every block, which would serve as a model. The provisions of the Tobacco Control Order would be used to enforce the penal and coercive measures to ban the sale of tobacco products or cigarettes within 100 metres of the school premises.

To begin with, the schools would find out the number of teachers, staffers and students addicted to tobacco and inform the administration at the start of the session. The administration would monitor the progress after four months and schools with good results would be declared "tobacco-free" and their success etched in the plaque.

Upadhyay said the idea behind displaying the plaque was to educate the students about their well being. The students would be spared coercive action like rustication.

Besides organising anti-tobacco programmes throughout the year, the school stationery would sport suitable slogans. Schools excelling in the programme would be honoured on the Republic Day.

Though schools would send monthly progress reports, the administration would carry out sudden inspections. District collectors and chief executive officers of district panchayats would also be involved in the implementation of the programme.

Heading: India plans to beef up security - Indian Express
Content:
To ensure that electricity along the border remains continuous, the Border Security Force (BSF) will be getting a special power supply line along the Akhnoor sector to Kathua from the State's Power Department. The move comes as a means to check militant infiltration that increases during the night.

Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of BSF, J B Sanghvan, said, "At the time of power breakdown we make use of the generators so that there was no infiltration. We even use the mobile generators."

According to officials. the proposal for the power supply line will be taken up by the BSF with the Power Development Department (PDD). " The supply line to the border as of now comes from sub transmission line-Ist and the BSF depends on generators for the illumination of the border," said Executive Engineer Division III, Power Development Department, M L Kalotra.

BSF personnel move along the border in armoured vehicles as well as engage in daily patrolling. Continuous power along the border is among the measures taken by the BSF as part of intensifying its vigil. Other steps include the deployment of more BSF personnel and modern gadgets to accentuate surveillance.

Heading: Why n-deal worries the league - Indian Express
Content:
After Monday's suicide attack on the Indian embassy killed four Indians, including a defence attaché, India is beefing up security at all its consulates in Afghanistan — Jalalabad, Kandahar, Herat and Mazar-e-Sharif — on war footing and is ensuring that they are strengthened as soon as possible to resist similar blasts.

With news reports — which have been dismissed by India as being baseless — appearing in the Pakistani media about a terror attack on it, the Jalalabad consulate is said to be under maximum threat. Even before these suspicious reports appeared, however, officials had put it on top of their watch list after specific intelligence reports received earlier this month. Although it has been doubly reinforced with a new bomb-resistant hexa barrier as well as a concrete barricade, this consulate's location, in a private building on a busy street, makes it even more vulnerable to attack. While the reports, which claimed that two Indians were killed in a suicide attack here, have been termed as "psychological warfare", India is taking no chances and has asked local authorities to block the street in front of the building and to restrict movements.

The Kandahar consulate, on the other hand, is located in a larger, more open area and is less vulnerable to attacks, but both Herat and Mazar-e-Sharif are considered unsafe.

What worries the Indian security establishment is the easy access that the ISI-backed Taliban militants have to Afghanistan through the Pakistan border. Officials say that the Kandahar jail breaks last month, where 30 motorcycle-borne attackers and two suicide bombers crossed the border and freed over 400 Taliban militants, once again accentuates how deeply the ISI is immersed in terrorist activities in the area.

In the meanwhile, the movements of the embassy staff have been restricted for a few days before a new security plan is implemented. While the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) personnel stay within the embassy, all other members of the staff reside in different, dispersed parts of the city, making them easy targets for attack. As a result, interim security arrangements are being worked out for them until the new embassy in Wazir Akbar Khan, which will be able to house most of the embassy staff, comes up.

Heading: Colonel faces UN probe for ‘backing’ armed group in Congo - Indian Express
Content:
The Indian Union Muslim League's decision to support the UPA Government in the nuclear deal has put the party in a tight spot in Kerala, its stronghold. The party, an ally of the Congress-led United Democratic Front in the state, is being pulled up by Muslim organisations, both mainstream and fringe, for supporting the Congress. These organisations have found the issue as a chance to storm into community bastions, whipping up anti-US sentiments and IUML's craze to wallow in power.

Besides, the IUML's stand has given the CPI(M)-led Left Democratic Front an opportunity to raise the anti-US plank in the ensuing Lok Sabha polls. CPI(M) state secretary Pinarayi Vijayan on Friday fired the first salvo against the IUML saying that by supporting the Congress, IUML had proved it was loyal to US imperialism.

People's Democratic Party chairman Abdul Nazar Ma'adani told The Indian Express that IUML had resorted to double standards on the issue. "The Muslim community across the world had been facing atrocities sponsored by the US. The deal with an anti-Muslim country should have been opposed by the IUML." He said IUML would have to pay for its reluctance to address the issue. On several issues, like the demolition of the Babri Masjid, IUML had failed to rise to the aspirations of the community, he said.

The anti-US sentiments being whipped up by Left parties and extremist Muslim outfits in the state would be a matter of concern for the IUML in the next election, when the party desperately needs an electoral comeback. The party had lost Manjeri Lok Sabha seat, its stronghold, in the 2004 election. Its worst electoral performance was in the state Assembly election held in 2006, when the party was pulverized by the Left and IUML rebels, who exposed the party's weakness in critical issues affecting the community.

The CPI(M) had played the anti-American strategy to the hilt twice in the recent past. During the Assembly election in 2006, the LDF had approached Muslim voters highlighting the Congress Government's pro-US stand and India's vote against Iran at the International Atomic Energy Agency.

In the bypoll to Thiruvambady Assembly constituency held in December, 2006, the LDF took up the issue of Saddam Hussein, served with death sentence then, to solicit Muslim votes for the CPI(M) candidate. The Left had emphasised the Congress-led UPA Government's failure to condemn the death sentence and flay the US for manipulating the case against the ousted Iraqi president. The Left played the anti-US trick, knowing very well that Saddam had been close to Muslim hearts. As expected, Saddam and a host of other factors helped the CPI(M) candidate scrape through in the bypoll.

The Left strategy to tap Muslims' anti-US feelings always stemmed from the helplessness of the IUML to react to all issues pertaining to the US and its imperialistic tendencies. IUML, being an ally of the Congress at the Centre and in Kerala as well, had been in a quandary to openly criticise the foreign policies of the Government.

"The nuclear deal would certainly influence the Muslim voters in the election. The Muslim community has always fought against imperialistic forces. That was why Saddam's death sentence and Iran issue had influenced the community in Kerala," said K T Jaleel, MLA and an IUML rebel, who defeated party state general secretary K P Kunhalikkuty in the Muslim-dominated Kuttipuram constituency in north Kerala.

IUML state secretary E T Muhammed Basheer told The Indian Express that the party had considered several other issues while deciding to support the Congress in the deal. "We have to ensure that communal forces do not return to power. The party has to look beyond the nuclear deal while taking a decision," he said.

Meanwhile, on July 2, CPI(M) mouthpiece Deshabhimani had carried an article, written by party MLA P Jayarajan, giving enough hints that the party would highlight the nuclear deal in Kerala as IUML's failure to stand up to American imperialism. The article said that IUML has double standards on the nuclear deal. It said the Congress was with the US, which had killed many in Iraq, Afghanistan and Palestine. Manmohan Singh, under duress from the America, was hell-bent on inking the deal. The IUML has been silent on the issue, even when dissenting voices against the deal have come from within the Congress and the UPA. The article, referring to League's silence on the nuclear issue, said IUML leaders in Kerala owe allegiance to America, Congress, power and money.

Heading: Assets case: Maya alleges political conspiracy - Indian Express
Content:
After three Indian peacekeepers were charged with illegally detaining and assaulting a local resident, the Indian peacekeeping mission in Congo has run into more trouble with a Colonel being investigated for making statements in support of an armed group.

The UN has started investigations against Colonel Chand Saroha, who was commanding a unit near Goma, for sympathising with the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP) led by General Laurent Nkunda at a public function in April.

The inquiry is being conducted on the basis of a recording of the meeting that is in possession of the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS). Reports say that the Colonel addressed Nkunda as a "brother" and expressed his support for the armed group's cause.

What has raised hackles in the UN is that such statements about armed groups are totally in contradiction to its rules and mandate in the country. While Saroha has said that his statements were independent and did not reflect the UN Mission in Congo, an inquiry has been instituted against him.

The incident, which had the potential of turning into a major political issue in the sensitive country, also forced the UN to express to the "high ranking authorities" of Congo "its total repudiation of the declarations and the regrettable personal behaviour of this officer".

While Saroha has since returned to India, the spokesperson of the UN Mission in Congo has said that all measures will be taken to sanction the officer for his serious indiscretion. "In the event of confirmation of the facts which were reported, MONUC intends to take all the necessary measures so that this officer is sanctioned in accordance with the procedures in force, for his serious deficiencies in his capacity as a peacekeeper after being delegated with authority by the mission," said the spokesperson.

The Colonel, meanwhile, will probably find it difficult to refute the charges since the UN possesses the voice and video recording of the controversial meeting.

Heading: Raj warns Marathi officials against aiding ‘outsiders’ - Indian Express
Content:
In response to reports that the CBI has sought permission from the Supreme Court to prosecute Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Mayawati in the disproportionate assets case, the UP Government, in a press release, has come out with a host of allegations against the investigative agency.

The UP Government has termed the filing of the counter-affidavit by the CBI a "political conspiracy" in keeping with the announcement made by Mayawati, while withdrawing support from the Central Government, that the CBI was being "pressurised" to implicate her.

Mayawati had, on a previous occasion, announced that the then NDA government also tried to pressurise her by misusing the CBI in 2003. "Several legal experts believe that filing of the counter-affidavit by the CBI, just a few days before the date when the UPA Government is expected to prove its majority on the floor of the House, casts a doubt on the action of the CBI," the press release states.

The conditional support extended by Mayawati's arch rivals, the Samajwadi Party, to the Congress is also cited as one of the reasons for questioning the CBI's actions. "The SP is believed to have sought action against the BSP supremo, who is a sworn opponent of the SP," the release says.

According to the UP Government, the CBI's filing of the affidavit in the SC 17 days before the due date of July 28, even though the case has been pending with the agency for years, is motivated by the factors listed above.

The CBI's decision to circulate copies of the affidavit to the media "even before its submission to the SC" has also drawn the ire of the UP Government. "Legal experts believe that all these actions cast doubt on the working of the CBI and substantiate the views expressed by Mayawati in her plea before the Supreme Court," the release adds.

Heading: 7/11: Rlys security plan on paper only - Indian Express
Content:
Maharashtra Navni-rman Sena (MNS) president Raj Thackeray on Friday gave a month's ultimatum to Marathi officials to stop helping influx of "outsiders" by issuing bogus domicile certificates, ration cards and driving licences. "I will communicate with you (Marathi officials) again after a month. If no action is taken from your end, the MNS will undertake the job of maintaining law and order," Raj said in a four-page statement after addressing party workers here. The statement came after a closed-door meeting of party functionaries at Ravindra Natya Mandir here.

The MNS chief also announced a helpline for reporting against outsiders. "I appeal to you to contact me on 9987999444, 9987999555 or mail me at reachrajthackeray@gmail.com if someone is forcing you to favour those from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar," he said.

Citing reasons for opposing migrant settlers from the two states, Raj said: "They create their vote bank and their leaders plan to illegally take over the state." He accused the 'bhaiyyas' from UP and Bihar of operating 20-50 taxis on each taxi permit and illegally grabbing land in the state.

Heading: Bhutan PM to visit India - Indian Express
Content:
Two years after the 7/11 attack, a suburban railway system where not much has changed in terms of security, and a Ministry, which is still dragging its feet on clearing an integrated security plan for important railway stations across the country—including Mumbai's suburban network — are stark realities for Mumbaikars, particularly for those 6.9 million people who take the local everyday.

Two years after seven blasts ripped apart trains, killing 187 people, the ordeal for Parag Sawant and Amit Singh is far from over. Both these men, in their twenties, are still undergoing treatment in local Mumbai hospitals. Both may have come out of comas, but cannot walk out of the hospital on their own. The only saving grace for their families is the fact that the cost of their treatment is being borne by the Railways, which has already reimbursed more than Rs 65 lakh on their hospital bills.

From putting five of the seven damaged coaches back on track to disbursing compensations worth Rs 25 crore to blast victims and their families, and absorbing 69 people from affected families into railway jobs, Railways has shown the intent and the will to deliver.

But it has failed in executing an effective security system at the 28 suburban stations of the Western Railways despite installing 530 CCTVs, 71 metal detectors and hiring 12 dog squads in addition to the Railways' five.

A proposal to engage private players on Build Own Operate and Transfer-basis to provide equipment for security and explosive detection and disposal are still being "discussed" in the corridors of Rail Bhavan. "Private players are lining up to install, operate and maintain the security apparatus. However, the Railway Board is yet to decide on the policy," a senior railway official told The Indian Express.

The Railway Protection Force (RPF), meanwhile, has some reason to cheer. Responding to its RPF Mitra (Friend) scheme, which envisages involving rail users in day-to-day surveillance activities, around 535 people have registered themselves in Mumbai. "Involving railway users in to gather information is the best way to prevent terror strikes. We plan to rope in more people for this scheme," an RPF official said.

Heading: CRI in Kasauli may re-open - Indian Express
Content:
Within two months of Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's Bhutan visit making him the first world leader to visit the new democracy, Bhutan Prime Minister Jigmi Y Thinley will visit India from July 14 to 17.

This would be his first visit outside Bhutan as the first democratically-elected Prime Minister after Bhutan's historic transition to a democratic constitutional monarchy.

During the visit, the Bhutan PM will call on President Pratibha Patil, Vice-President Hamid Ansari and will hold talks with Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi, External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee, Leader of Opposition L K Advani and Planning Commission deputy chairman Montek Singh Ahluwalia will call on him.

The PM will also host a state banquet in honour of the visiting dignitary.

The Bhutanese PM will be accompanied by a high-level delegation including Economic Affairs Minister Khandu Wangchuck, Foreign Affairs Minister Ugyen Tshering, Finance Minister Wangdi Norbu and other senior officials from the Royal Government of Bhutan, the Ministry of External Affairs statement said on Friday.

"India and Bhutan share very special relations which have roots in our history and culture," the statement added.

Heading: The city of contradictions - Indian Express
Content:
While the Union Health Ministry has ruled out the possibility of producing DPT vaccine and yellow fever vaccine at the Central Research Institute, Kasauli, it is likely to restart the unit for serum production.

In a recent report submitted to the Health Secretary, the Drug Controller General of India (DGCI), who visited the institute to check if re-structuring of the unit was possible to conform to Indian Good Manufacturing practices, has said it is possible to produce serum at the unit.

"We have just got the report which says that there is a possibility of producing anti-rabies vaccines and anti-venom serum at CRI, Kasauli," Naresh Dayal, Health Secretary, told The Indian Express.

The Ministry had suspended the licenses of three PSUs — BCG Vaccine laboratory at Guindy, Chennai, Pasteur Institute, Coonoor, and the Central Research Institute, Kasauli in January this year after the WHO pointed out that the PSUs did not meet statutory requirements. Even though the international health agency offered to upgrade the technology at these PSUs, the Health Ministry decided against it and shut down the units.

Heading: Fear stalks Jharkhand politicians - Indian Express
Content:
Theka sharaab desi — that ubiquitous liquor vend found in almost all cities — is conspicuous by its absence in Chandigarh. The city hasn't been adapted by Alcoholic Anonymous and maintains a hearty appetite for all things intoxicating. Some months ago, the Union Territory Administration issued a dictum that liquor shops in the city should do away with their hideous desi appellations. They were to call themselves Taverns, just like they do in London!

This is one example of a series of measures announced by the UT Administration in the last two years, which has been copied from first-world cities. Per se, there is nothing wrong in adapting measures that can ensure a better standard of life for people, but qualitatively, the life of the people of Chandigarh hasn't improved, as they continue to grapple with problems that remain unaddressed. As such, the administration's new fangled schemes appear hollow and exclusivist.

For instance, no one objects to the introduction of New York's poop-the-scoop law, which requires city denizens to clean-up after their pet has soiled the road. But, such laws appear superficial when the administration has been unable to control the menace of street dogs and loose cattle that not only dirty the streets but also cause casualties and injuries.

Similarly, authorities show a zealous obsession to maintain the congruity of buildings in terms of shape, size and colour. Two days ago, when DAV Sector 10, the city's best-known college, changed the paint of its facade, the administration showed amazing alacrity in issuing it a notice. Taj Hotels had a harrowing time to get approval for their building plans as the height of their hotel contravened the city's idea of symmetry. This suggests an attempt to maintain and guard the architectural legacy of Le Corbusier, the French architect who designed the city. In fact, the administration went to the extent of filing an application for grant of world heritage site status by UNESCO to the city. But the same administration also showed such a blatant apathy to furniture designed by Corbusier that they were sold as scrap. These items were subsequently bought by connoisseurs for several thousand dollars at international auctions.

An order to make Chandigarh the first smoke-free city in the country (no smoking in public places) appears ludicrous in view of an inability to control pollution by city's traffic which threatens to become unmanageable in a couple of years.

Even Sukhna Lake, the city's best-known landmark, is getting the worst of such quixotic ideas. Inspired by the Dutch countryside, the administration has installed a pseudo windmill that consumes more power than it generates. It has also started shikara rides akin to Srinagar. But it has miserably failed to control the dramatic shrinking and depletion of the lake. The water has sunk to such an abysmal level that the very existence of Sukhna is threatened.

The UT's councillors and officers make foreign trips on pretexts as flimsy as the need to check the working of an imported road-cleaning machine and toy with the idea of automated sabzi mandi even when the roofs of existing ones are falling and killing people. It might want to be perceived as world-class city, but Chandigarh fails to match up to a yardstick that is associated with all the great cities of world — a cosmopolitan culture that facilitates fulfilling of dreams by welcoming ambitious people. It reserves 85 per cent of the seats in its colleges for local students and as per it MP's own admission, its infrastructure is not exactly prepared to handle the rush of professionals concomitant with the setting up of a new IT park.

Heading: I haven’t quit, insists Charlesworth - Indian Express
Content:
Jharkhand's politicians are living in constant fear — particularly the Adivasi, the Dalit and OBC leaders who had dared to help the police against the Maoists.

Take the case of 40-year-old ward councillor Ashok Munda (name changed). This Adivasi leader, who also owns a petrol pump, is terrified of the Maoists. At a private gathering, he may call them 'extortionists' and 'murderers', in public gatherings he avoids even mentioning them. Always accompanied by armed securitymen, he has turned his office into a fortress. "Most of us do not feel safe even with two to three securitymen guarding us. The Army should comb each and every home to nab them," he says in a hushed voice.

He is not alone; his colleagues, too, are scared of antagonising Kundan Pahan and his men.

JD(U) MLA and former minister Ramesh Singh Munda, who was shot dead on July 9, was on the hit list of the Naxalites. He had allegedly not paid the entire amount that he had promised them prior to winning the Tamar constituency seat in 2005.

CPI(ML) MLA Mahendra Singh, JMM MP Sunil Mahato and Anup Marandi, son of former chief minister Babulal Marandi, had challenged the Maoists in their respective constituencies and were shot dead by the rebels on January 16, 2005, March 4, 2007 and October 26, 2007, respectively.

Killing of these leaders and that of 200 policemen since 2000 has prompted several politicians to stop touring the interior areas of their constituencies. Those who represent Naxal-infested constituencies (70 out of the total 81) are not stepping out of their homes and night outings are as good as over.

"I used to go for morning walks in the open Morahabadi ground. But due to security reasons, I have started going for morning strolls inside the Army cantonment in Deepatoli," said leader of opposition and former chief minister Arjun Munda.

"President's rule should be imposed without any delay," said RJD MLA Anapurna Devi. This was reiterated by Congress MP Furkhan Ansari, who said, "delay in doing so will only worsen the scene." BJP's chief whip C P Singh had an identical demand. "No one knows when they will strike," he said.

Suman Mahato, JMM MP and wife of Sunil Mahato, has instructed her staff not to let strangers inside her residence and has stopped touring Naxal-infested areas of her Jamshedpur constituency. "I do not know when this terror will end," she said.

And with politicians keeping away from such areas of their constituencies, the space is left vacant for the Naxals to further perpetrate their own brand of "politics".

Heading: Indian officials never wanted him - Indian Express
Content:
Indian hockey's great revival dream under Ric Charlesworth is clearly headed for a premature end, even as confusion reigned on Friday over the Australian advisor's resignation with the story veering around two letters and a denial.

While the sports ministry officials and members of the ad-hoc committee formed by the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) confirmed that Charlesworth had indeed quit, the man himself refuted reports that he had packed his bags and headed to Australia for good. Talking to The Indian Express from Melbourne, he said: "I've no idea and I don't know what to say. I have come to Australia for a personal and very important dinner (as a member of the Sports Australia Hall of Fame) and to see my mother. I always made it clear that I was to return to India on the 26th, and I will be returning. Things are difficult... you know how things work in India. But the sports ministry and all other officials concerned know what the exact situation is, so I don't know what the confusion is about," Charlesworth said, adding that the reports in India "sure aren't coming from me".

"I guess I will have to put up an official statement to clear all the rumours. Also, there is nothing clear on who is handling what, I don't know who is running the game in the country, who I report to — things are very unclear," he added.

Charlesworth's frustration, which had been clear for several weeks, had led him to write a couple of letters to the powers that be in Indian hockey. The first was addressed to RK Naidu, Sports Authority of India's (SAI) executive director (team wings), and stated: "I have attached my resignation as I do not believe in continuing in an environment where there is no support. I cannot see how anything more can be achieved in my present position."

In the second letter — his official resignation note (box, right) — Charlesworth spoke in detail about the problems he faced in India and about how he always knew that "India would be difficult... I just did not believe it could be this difficult." One of Charlesworth's key concerns was the lack of payment still due to him from India, as had been first reported by The Indian Express on June 20.

But, when asked specifically whether he has put in his papers and bid farewell to India, Charlesworth said on Friday there had been no decision as yet. Perhaps a change of heart over the last fortnight.

It is clear, however, that Indian hockey officials are more than happy to see Charlesworth go. While IOA officials repeatedly referred to the letter of resignation when asked about Charlesworth's status, not willing to entertain the possibility of a change of heart on the Australian's part, selection committee chairman Aslam Sher Khan said the call to take was not whether Charlesworth was ready to stay in India but whether India was ready for him. "Ric wants a completely professional set-up in Indian hockey and has a long-term plan. But more than him making us world champions, we have to decide whether we are ready to be world champions," Aslam said.

There is, however, the problem of the World Cup that will have to be addressed if Charlesworth does indeed leave.
