Meanwhile, the Nepali Congress (NC), the second largest party in the Constituent Assembly, reiterated its demand that Prime Minister Girija Prasad Koirala be made the country's first president. "The party will otherwise sit in the opposition and play a constructive role in drafting the new constitution," NC Vice President Prakash Man Singh said.

The Constituent Assembly passed the Fifth Amendment to the constitution on Sunday. It focuses on changing the provision requiring two-thirds majority to form government, with the simple majority.

The amendment paves the way for Maoists to lead the next administration. The Maoist and the CPN-UML have a combined strength of 337 in the 601-strong assembly.

Heading: How they miss Surjeet - Indian Express
Content:
A hostage drama in which junior officials of the Nepal police held at least seven of their seniors captive for 39 hours in Anke district, some 500 km west from here, came to an end with the surrender of the rebels around midnight on Sunday.

Sub-Inspector Dhan Bahadur B K, who led the revolt along with ten others, has been arrested. "They are being tried as per the police act," Police headquarters said. The police operation to quell the revolt — the third one in the past three weeks in the security agencies — was assisted by the Nepal army.

The junior officials and jawans had held seven officers including a senior superintendent of the police in the police headquarters alleging that they ill-treated the juniors and that sub-standard ration was being supplied to subordinates.

Heading: Speaking freely - Indian Express
Content:
Amdist the great excitement about the July 22 confidence vote, escalating polemics between the Congress and the comrades and the worldwide publicity to the India-specific safeguards agreement with the IAEA that Foreign Minister Pranab Mukherjee had adamantly held to be "confidential", one important and instructive facet of the high drama and low comedy has not received the attention it deserves. It is the trajectory of the shifting relationship between Indian communists and the Indian National Congress that, ironically, has come full circle and is back to where it was at the time of Independence: one of total opposition. There is one crucial difference, however: this time round armed rebellion — the reference being to Telengana, Kakdweep, Malabar, Tripura and so on (circa 1948) — is not on the agenda.

Ironically, P.C. Joshi, the first general secretary of the then undivided Communist Party of India (CPI), who really built it up and extended its influence far beyond its ranks, saw the convergence between nationalism and communism, and advocated a policy of "all support to Nehru". This was an act of courage because the communists, having been a part of nationalist struggle until World War II, became votaries of "people's war" after Hitler's invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, and later opposed vehemently the 1942 Quit India Movement.

Joshi was immediately repudiated, reprimanded, humiliated and hounded out. The hardline B.T. Ranadive took over. This change was inevitable because of the finality of the Soviet Communist Party's (in reality Stalin's) "advice" to "fraternal parties". Echoing Stalin, and even Mao, the CPI maintained that Indian independence was a "sham", which is what CPM General Secretary Prakash Karat is saying today in the context of the Indo-US nuclear deal. The CPI of yore maintained its 1948 line up to 1955 when its thinking started changing under the impact of India's China policy, the Bandung Conference and, above all, the warming of Indo-Soviet relations.

It is very significant therefore that on December 12, 1955, in his talks with the visiting Soviet leaders, Nikolai Bulganin and Nikita Khrushchev, Jawaharlal Nehru firmly, if politely, raised the question of the CPI's "role". He began by saying that because "it (CPI's role) was coming in conflict with the nationalist sentiment", ill feelings were created and "many opportunities of cooperation were lost". (Isn't Prime Minister Manmohan Singh saying roughly the same thing today?) Nehru drove home two points: that the CPI took "direction" from the Soviet Union, and that it was getting "considerable sums of money from outside". In support of his first contention, he cited chapter and verse, including the revelation that after a meeting of four Indian communists "with Mr Stalin" in 1951, the line laid down was of "full opposition to government, and where possible, petty insurrections". In September 1955, Nehru added, communist leader Ajoy Ghosh had gone to Moscow and come back with "fresh instructions" — "to play down opposition to government, but must be ready to start insurrection again when necessary".

Khrushchev, of course, denied everything his host had said, adding that though he knew "Mr Ghosh by name", he had never met him. The Indian communist leader might have met "Stalin, who was a great man", but what Ghosh had reportedly "attributed to Stalin" was not correct.

Unfortunately, for 47 long years there was not a whiff about this crucial Nehru-Khrushchev conversation. A record of it was published only in 2002 in the 31st volume of Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Second Series. Moscow, by then, was indifferent to the history of the Soviet era. Some Indian CPI leaders did demur. But they were quickly silenced. The late Mohit Sen's memoirs gave a graphic description of the secret journey of Ajoy Ghosh, S.A. Dange, C. Rajeswara Rao and M. Basavapunniah to the Soviet Union on a Russian ship and of their meetings with Stalin and other Soviet leaders. Sen's account confirmed Nehru and confuted Khrushchev. It was precisely then that the Telengana revolt was called off.

Reverting to the chronology of events, as the decade of the '50s drew to a close and the crisis with China, leading to the 1962 war, mounted, tensions between the Congress and the communists inevitably grew. Two years later, the party was split into the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and the CPI. This took place in the context of the wide Sino-Soviet split. The CPI remained loyal to the Soviet Union. But to call the CPM as wholly pro-Chinese, as most people did then, was perhaps an exaggeration.

To go over all the twists and turns in the relations between the two communist parties and the Congress on the one hand and the terribly complex relationship of conflict and cooperation between the two brands of communists on the other would require a tome. Suffice it to say that the CPI had been broadly supportive of the Congress, especially of Indira Gandhi, while the CPM had been generally hostile. In 1970, just before opting for Lok Sabha elections a year before schedule, Indira Gandhi ensured that CPI leader Achchutha Menon headed Kerala's coalition ministry to which the Congress provided the ballast. Some comrades foolishly started conjuring up the tantalising vision of the "Kerala pattern being replicated in New Delhi".

With the CPM leadership passing from E.M.S. Namboodiripad to Harkishan Singh Surjeet, the Marxist party's policies took a "pragmatic turn". So it was that both the communist parties supported the V.P. Singh government that depended for its survival also on backing by the BJP.

If Surjeet could have had his way, in 1996, the Vajpayee government would almost certainly have been replaced by a non-BJP government, headed by Jyoti Basu. It was Karat who put paid to the exercise, something Basu was to call later a "historic blunder". Now, as then, Karat is steadfastly sticking to the "hard line". Indeed, he is unmoved even though Basu has yet again made no secret of his unhappiness. Karat's colleagues in the Marxist politburo, Sitaram Yechury and Biman Bose, were content to be in London at this critical juncture. And CPI General Secretary A.B. Bardhan, even while pronouncing anathema on the "deceitful government", is talking of "cooperation" with the Congress in future. But then, all this is the nature of the beast called Indian politics.

The writer is a political commentator indermalhotra30@hotmail.com

Heading: Maya’s verdicts - Indian Express
Content:
There is a temptation to dismiss the clouds of controversy swirling around the speaker's chair as dust kicked up by politics-as-usual. This would be a grievous error. The office of speaker is one of the few political institutions that have been strengthened, rather than weakened, by the rough-and-tumble of legislative politics. Initially, the speaker was seen by the parliamentary opposition as following the government's instructions; the very first motion of no-confidence in a Lok Sabha speaker was submitted barely two years into the first Lok Sabha. Over time, however, as the power of the majority party has fractured, the position has gained in power, independence and stature. Since Balram Jakhar's tenure (1984-89), the occupants of the speaker's chair have been very careful about ensuring both the appearance and actuality of independence and of insulation from mundane political pressures. This extended even to moments of crisis, when cabinets were toppling: some of the most enduring memories of the dramatic 1999 vote of no-confidence against the Vajpayee government, which failed by one vote, are of the strict neutrality that was evident in G.M.C. Balayogi's various rulings.

This painstakingly crafted consensus is still tenuous, and it would be very unfortunate if the Left's decision to declare that the speaker is subject to their party whip were to undermine it. The Left's claimed distaste for the trappings of bourgeois democracy apart, it has largely shown itself to be the group most respectful of parliamentary procedure and the institutions of civilised debate. This reputation, as well, is under threat. In addition, to force their most distinguished parliamentarian to choose between the institution which he has served faithfully and the party to which he has pledged allegiance is an act of great and cynical unkindness. Somnath Chatterjee must be dismayed at the prospect: now that that all-important Stalinist phrase, the internal discipline of the Party, has been invoked, he must either betray his party or his principles. These are not the acts of a mature political grouping.

Chatterjee has not been a perfect speaker; the respect commanded on all sides of the House by his long career as a legislator apart, he is not the best manager of people that the chair has seen in recent times. However, that he has been non-partisan is not doubted by anyone. His tenure as speaker and his record as an ordinary member of the House deserve a better end than one that weakens the structure of Parliament.

Heading: Testing each other’s limits - Indian Express
Content:
Memories are famously short in politics. So the CPM has forgotten the ludicrous allegation many moons ago that BSP founder Kanshi Ram was a "CIA agent", and its general secretary, Prakash Karat, drove down to Mayawati's residence to forge understanding with the BSP on how to vote out the UPA government — and presumably, with it, the Indo-US nuclear deal. Changing partners has never frazzled Mayawati,

but she has had some amnesiac moments too this week. Just over a month ago, when the Noida police were competing amongst themselves to mishandle the Arushi Talwar murder case, Mayawati, as Uttar Pradesh chief minister, asked for CBI intervention. It was not the first time that the executive needed the bureau to gain an aura of credibility and end a controversy. But look what Mayawati says now.

Now that the CBI has indicated in the Supreme Court that it has sufficient evidence to file a chargesheet against Mayawati for having assets disproportionate to her known sources of income, she is crying foul against the agency. And since this is a month for polarised, sharpened loyalties, she finds an echo from the left and right. The CBI, they all say, is playing to its susceptibility for political manipulation by targeting her. They say that Mulayam Singh Yadav's move to the Congress's side explains the almost simultaneous CBI move against her. It is, of course, entirely overlooked that the CBI has gathered copious evidence of assets to support its words in the apex court. Moreover, all these months, Mayawati has been filing objections against the CBI. To the CBI's affidavit in the court are appended her petitions and the CBI's counter-points.

Why then does Mayawati's charge find such political resonance? Of course, vendetta or the whiff of it is manna for a sharp politician. But the bureau too needs to introspect. There is perhaps little that it can do about the fact that many of the references that come to it may be motivated to suit the executive masters of the day. But the CBI has done little to assert or to be seen to assert the autonomy hard-won for it in the course of the hawala case in the mid-'90s.

Heading: Their valley of peace - Indian Express
Content:
Things are rapidly coming to a head in West Asia. Last month, Israel conducted long-range air exercises over the Mediterranean, interpreted as a signal that Iran should desist from the trajectory upon which they are accused of having set their nuclear programme. For all practical purposes, it was a dress rehearsal; should permission be given soon to attack Iran's nuclear facilities, both the Israeli and US administrations want the IDF to be ready. Many, in fact, view the present period of presidential transition in America as the most opportune from Israel's viewpoint for attacking Iran; a possible Obama administration, it is feared, might not be as sympathetic to Israeli concerns as the present administration.

This weekend, it was the Iranians' turn to rattle a few sabres. As part of naval exercises at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran test-fired a number of missiles over two successive days, including some that are capable of striking Israel. These tests follow a warning from Iran earlier that Tehran would strike Tel Aviv and American interests in West Asia if attacked. While this last development can be read essentially as Iran trying to manufacture a deterrent, there is nevertheless real danger from this escalation of the confrontation already under way between Iran and the West over its nuclear programme.

Details about the recent tests will take some time to confirm; doubts are already emerging about Iranian claims, given the fact that one of the pictures of the missiles taking off was apparently doctored. However, it appears that the missiles tested were both long- and medium-range, including the Shahab-3, which can reportedly hit targets over a distance of 2000 km, and can carry nuclear warheads.

This is the reason why the tests are causing jitters in West Asian and Western capitals. Negotiations between the West and Iran over its nuclear programme are going nowhere, with Iran making it clear once again last week that it would not comply with Security Council resolutions requiring it to stop enriching uranium. Frustration is growing in London, Paris and Berlin over what they view as Iranian intransigence. In a sign of the Europeans tightening the screws on Tehran, the Sarkozy government put pressure on Total, the French energy corporation, to cancel its plans to develop one of Iran's natural gas fields.

Talk continues to emerge from sections of the Washington establishment, particularly from the vice-president's office, of possible direct military action. However, the US's December 2007 National Intelligence Estimate concluded that Iran had halted its work on nuclear weapons in 2003, a finding which makes the possibility of military action somewhat remote. Instead, reports have emerged of the US Congress funding a major escalation of covert operations against Iran, designed to destabilise the country's religious leadership as demanded by the Bush administration.

In the meantime, Iran's 3800 centrifuges continue to spin, building up its supplies of low-enriched uranium. It is projected that, by the end of next year, Iran will have acquired enough such material to convert into sufficient highly enriched uranium for a nuclear weapon. This is what worries Israel: its exercises were to demonstrate its readiness to launch air-strikes if Iran were to cross the nuclear threshold. They were also aimed at putting pressure on the international community to do something about what the Israelis consider an existential threat. Israel has now responded to the Iranian missile tests by putting on display one of its aircraft that it says can spy on Iran.

Iran's missile tests are a signal to the world that it is a rising regional power that will follow its own interests and can no longer be pushed around. And, in case his adversaries didn't get the point of the tests, a commander of the Revolutionary Guard, Hossein Salami, underlined it: "Our hands are always on the trigger." It is also possible that Iran is feeling squeezed by economic sanctions; its aggressive posturing may be an attempt to cover up its weaknesses, lest its adversaries be tempted to further pressurise it.

Whatever the case may be, the region is once again on the edge with a real sense of looming crisis. Both sides are loath to compromise, for fear that their credibility would be affected. The danger to the world is that, amidst this back and forth between the two sides, either might overplay its hand or misread a signal. And if that happens, the mess in Iraq and Afghanistan would end up being a sideshow.

The writer teaches at King's College, London harsh.pant@kcl.ac.uk

Heading: Why Obama needs Europe - Indian Express
Content:
I visited Kashmir 46 years ago, then as an army officer's daughter. We were part of a large army convoy, traversing the snow-clad mountains and a series of tunnels. I have a faint memory of an ambience pregnant with attrition and armour-laden apprehension, as humongous camouflaged trucks wound their way into the valley of fear.

So the image of Kashmir I conjured up till now was not only from the attic of my memory, but also from the media of a perpetual war-weary zone. It bore the scars of the violence and the charred impact of gunpowder. The Valley's vicissitudes have been turbulent because of its volatile location and Hellenesque beauty. The K-word has had odious connotations in Indo-Pak peace negotiations, as it signals an inevitable deadlock.

I visited the Valley again recently, and was surprised to see that the guns have been silenced, war-ravaged buildings have been refurbished and new houses are appearing everywhere. The presence of armed forces has been minimised and the camouflaged patches have eased out. So I soaked in the idyllic scene of the shimmering Dal Lake, dotted with its filmi shikaras. There are patches of radiant peaks and white lotuses as well. In the backdrop sit houseboats with exotic names, and nature looms large with the encircling cordon of pine-covered mountains. Sometimes, in the limpid water (the lake has been cleaned), there are visible seaweeds and buoyant fish, and here and there on roadsides are riots of colourful flowers, enhancing the picture-postcard beauty. There are spates of tourists savouring the pristine air and enacting the roles of Hindi film stars in Kashmir ki wadiyan.

Whenever I looked at the calm mountainside, watching the pines sway back and forth, and experiencing the serenity calm water bodies exude, an old thought came back: How could this epitome of peace trigger so much violence? Whether truculent politicians, soldiers and clandestine agencies augur peace in this terrain, every tree, mountain and water body seem to cherish its tranquillity, as do its people. For them, in that fragile moment of stability — which one hopes will not be betrayed by the turn of events since then — lay the fervent hope that it never again became the veritable tinderbox it once was.

Heading: Individuals in focus - Indian Express
Content:
Barack Obama is coming to Europe. [He] has had a rough couple of weeks that have seen his steady six-point lead over John McCain cut nearly in half. [After] a handful of pirouettes on certain issues [Obama] is now seen by just more than half of Americans as someone who will tailor his positions for political advantage. McCain has done just as much so-called flip-flopping, if not more. And there is this difference between the two: whereas Obama's "refinements" [have] been toward the centre... McCain's have been entirely towards the far right. [He] has abandoned the views that once marked him as a Republican maverick, and embraced the Bush agenda. Most of the media [have] failed to note this utterly crucial distinction. The result is that Obama has paid a higher price for his changes than McCain has.

[So] Obama needs an event that can break this narrative. [The] domestic impact of Obama's trip will pry open a window on to [the] fundamental question of this campaign... To wit: has Bush failed so completely that Americans are ready to reject many of the conservative assumptions that have governed their thinking since Ronald Reagan's ascendancy...? Asked more directly: have Bush's failures been failures of ideology or merely of competence? If the former, [then] we can feel pretty safe predicting a smashing Democratic victory. If the latter, though, it could mean that voters are still OK with conservative governance — they just want someone who will administer it competently.

It's the dominant open question of this race. Here's where Europe fits in. Six years ago, no prominent Democrat would have set foot in France or Germany. [They] were "old Europe". Enemies of freedom. [With] this trip, Obama wants to signal: "No more of that. I will govern an America that will commit itself to liberal internationalism again..." [If] the trip is gaffe-free, he will be received by adoring crowds. [He] and his people surely hope that the images of those swooning crowds, transmitted back to America, will remind his countrymen [of] Bush's worst failures, and why they were in fact failures of ideology and not merely of competence... And, team Obama hopes, Americans will say to themselves: "Yes, that was a disgrace. No more of that. I'm with Obama."

Excerpted from a comment by Michael Tomasky in 'The Guardian'

Heading: CPI leader’s death rocks Assam House on day 1 - Indian Express
Content:
•Shekhar Gupta's emphasis on the personality factor was accurate 'Single personality disorder'. The Left seems to be governed by the intransigence of one individual, Prakash Karat. The BJP cannot strengthen the PM's hands because the "wrong person" is negotiating the deal. But L.K. Advani, another individual, lacks Vajpayee's vision about long-term national interests that should transcend short-term party interests.

Manmohan Singh's only fault is that he is an apolitical person who rose to power thanks to his political bosses. His only initiative was on the nuclear deal, which he discharged professionally. The draft leaves little to be desired and there was no forum more appropriate than the G8 summit for publicising the IAEA submission. This determined action from the single individual, Singh, is the biggest triumph. It will show that he was, after all, not a weak PM.

— A.N. Mitra

Delhi

•Shekhar Gupta's article was thought-provoking. However, it has to be acknowledged that Manmohan Singh was always perceived to be a de jure, and not the de facto, PM. This tempted his colleagues, UPA constituents, the Left and the BJP to attack him. Singh deserves credit for holding on and discharging his duties fairly well. Likewise, he has handled the nuclear deal wisely. Singh's critics couldn't stomach this fact. When these people could not target the deal any longer, they resorted to criticising the person behind the deal. If the deal wins, history will judge the PM rightly.

— H.S. Gur Hisar

Population engineering?

•This refers to 'Fertility rate in India still very high: experts'. Family planning in India was voluntarily adopted by the educated middle class. There are few middle-class families with more than two children. But the poor and illiterate didn't or couldn't do so. Therefore, their families continued to expand and they have failed to secure their children education and other necessities. Educated and healthy people are a nation's assets. Clearly, India's population explosion is parallelled by a proportionate drop in talent. In place of population control, the government should extend its mission from family planning to population planning by providing health and education services to the poor and illiterate, where such benefits are linked to their family size.

— Hara Lal Chakraborty

Kolkata

Entrenched minorities

•Pratap Bhanu Mehta has rightly observed that "The concept of secular citizenship is almost dead in India" 'Partitions of the mind', . In a secular democracy, the concepts of majority and minority relate to the numbers subscribing to a particular policy or ideology. But in India, we have entrenched majorities and minorities based on caste and community, which can never alter. Thus, instead of a nation of citizens, we've become a conglomeration of castes and communities. The caste and communal consciousness has replaced the sense of national unity.

— P.R. Dubhashi

Pune

Heading: Don’t attend session, ethics committee tells Ripun Bora - Indian Express
Content:
The Opposition staged a walkout on Monday in the Assam Assembly after they failed to move an adjournment motion on the prevailing law and order situation in the state.

Leader of Opposition Chandra Mohan Patowari moved the adjournment motion to discuss the death of senior CPI leader from Morigaon, Manoj Deka on July 4 allegedly after being brutally assaulted by police constable Rafiqul Islam. He said it was not an ordinary incident and smacked of political conspiracy.

Deka, state committee member and secretary of the CPI's Morigaon district unit, suffered head injuries after he was assaulted by Islam, a PSO of Kamal Bora, the officer in-charge of Morigaon police station on July 1. He died three days later.

"The Congress-led Government of Tarun Gogoi has failed to provide security to life and property of the common man which is evident from the fact that a constable could assault a senior and prominent citizen of a small district town leading to his death," Patowari said. He also referred to several incidents including the death of a namghoria (village priest) who was allegedly assaulted by Army personnel in Sivasagar recently and the attacks on former Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) cadres by NDFB militants. "The common man is today living under the fear of death," he said.

"Assam's overall law and order situation is turning from bad to worse under the Gogoi government, and this is evident from the recent report of the Union Home Ministry," Patowari said.

He said the state Government was taken for a ride by the Dima Halam Daoga (DHD) which had stalled construction on the four-lane East-West Corridor and a broad gauge railway track in the NC Hills district, and said that the Government was a "total failure."

Echoing his views veteran CPI leader Drupad Bargohain lambasted the Gogoi government. "While most of the political leaders killed in Assam in the past were victims of militant attacks, Manoj Deka's is the first instance of a policeman killing a political leader," Bargohain said. He also asked why the officer whose PSO had killed Deka, was not yet arrested.

Other senior opposition leaders including Mission Ranjan Das (BJP), Uddhab Barman (CPI-M) and Aditya Langthasa (AUDF) joined Patowari to move the adjournment motion and criticised the Government over the issue.

Speaking on behalf of the Chief Minister, Forest and Tourism Minister Rockybul Hussain, said the state Government had already ordered a judicial probe into the incident headed by a retired High Court judge." If the Opposition wants we can even go for an inquiry commission headed by a sitting judge," Health Minister H B Sharma said.

The Government named former High Court judge P C Phukan to head inquiry commission and asked him to wind up the probe within six months. The notice was issued on July 1, Sharma added.

Heading: Kargil’s first Indian PoW back in sky, to fly mid-air refuellers - Indian Express
Content: The Committee on Ethics of Assam Assembly has requested arrested MLA and former minister Ripun Bora not to attend  the ongoing monsoon session. Former Education minister Bora was arrested by the CBI for trying to bribe one of its officers. Speaker Tanka Bahadur Rai said that entry of an elected person cannot be barred and the Committee has, therefore, requested him not to attend the Assembly session.

Heading: Dowry cases treble in Assam in 7 years - Indian Express
Content:
First Indian Prisoner of War (PoW) in the Kargil conflict, Kambampati Nachiketa, is all set to fly mid-air refuellers — a small consolation for him after an injury caused by "physical hardships" during captivity kept him away from operating fighter aircraft.

"I am being transferred to Air Force Station Agra next month. Now I'll be flying IL-78 air-to-air refuellers," said Nachiketa, who was captured by Pakistani forces on May 27, 1999 after his MiG-27 suffered a flame-out while destroying enemy positions in the Batalik sub-sector.

On that fateful day, Nachiketa, then a flight lieutenant, took off in a 'Hayena' formation led by Sqn Ldr A Mandhokot to bomb enemy positions with 80 mm canons.

Despite initial difficulties, the Vayu Sena Medal awardee identified the target and fired 40 rockets in one salvo and attacked again, this time with 30 mm guns. "I then eased out of the dive, but felt a backward jerk due to sudden deceleration. The speed dropped to 500 kmph and I realised that the engine had flamed out. I immediately jettisoned the rocket pods and attempted a relight. Informing my leader Sqn Ldr Mandhokot, I further lowered the altitude to maintain the speed which had fallen to 450 kmph," he said.

With hills surrounding the area and no sign of the engine restarting, Nachiketa realised that eviction was inevitible and pulled the ejection handle.

While ejecting, Nachiketa saw his aircraft crash into the hills and go up in flames. "After about 15 seconds of para descent, I landed on soft ice. I saw people running towards me. Bullets were being fired and I returned the fire from the small arms I was carrying. After holding forth for some time, there was an ambush and I was made a PoW," he said. Now a Wing Commander, Nachiketa was unwilling to discuss his experience during captivity but said he was made to undergo "physical hardships".

"It is an experience which is difficult to be described in words. Sometimes I felt that death would have been a better solution," he said. He now suffers from back pain and this prevents him from flying a fighter plane. Doctors attribute his pain to the injury during para-landing and the physical hardships during captivity.

Besides physical scars, the experience had been traumatic psychologically. "It took quite some time to heal. But in two or three years you reconcile with life and get on with it." However, he said, "As a soldier, I am trained to bear this. The trauma had been bigger for my family."

"When you are in the cockpit, you have a role. Sometimes experience changes you so much that you accept whatever role you get. My experience has taught me not to regret what I have lost. It has made me stronger," Nachiketa, fondly known by friends and colleagues as 'Nachi' said.

Heading: MPA calls urgent meet on power deals - Indian Express
Content:
The number of dowry-related incidents has trebled in just seven years in Assam.

Statistics laid down by Information and Public Relations Minister Rockybul Hussain in the Assembly on Monday said while the number of dowry-related incidents had skyrocketed since Tarun Gogoi took over as Chief Minister in 2001, the number of rape cases had doubled during this period. He was replying to a question by Alaka Sharma (AGP).

While Assam registered 1,307 dowry-related cases in 2001, the figure went up to 3,063 in 2007. Similarly, cases of rape increased from 785 in 2001 to 1,311 in 2007. This year, already 505 cases have been reported in the first five months.

Incidents of trafficking have also recorded an alarming upward trend -- from six cases in 2001 to 23 last year.

Replying to another question by Ramendra Narayan Kalita (AGP), the minister said a total of 33 women had been raped by security personnel since 2001. Of them, 13 were raped by Army personnel, five by members of para-military forces and the remaining by policemen.

The minister said the Government had taken a number of steps to control crime against women. These included setting up of all-women police stations, establishment of a woman counselling centre at the Assam Police CID headquarters. The police had been directed to speedily dispose of cases related to crime against women.

Heading: Manipur militant groups accused of recruiting schoolchildren - Indian Express
Content:
Under pressure from its own allies and NGOs, the Meghalaya Progressive Alliance (MPA) Government has called a meeting on Monday night to discuss whether six power deals, signed by the previous government with private companies, should be scrapped.

The UDP had recently held a meeting where workers most of the alliance partners, including NCP, UDP, BJP, Khun Hynniewtrep National Awakening Movement (KHNAM) and Hills State People's Democratic Party (HSPDP), felt that the power deal must be scrapped irrespective of what the Cabinet feels.

State NCP president W R Kharlukhi has said in no uncertain terms that the power deal must be scrapped despite senior party leader and Power Minister Conrad K Sangma announcing that the Cabinet will take a decision keeping in mind the "best interests of the state".

The previous Congress-led MDA government had signed a Memorandum of Agreement with Jaypee Group, Dharampal Satyapal Group, ETA Star infrastructure Limited, Athena Project Private Limited, Seven Sisters Energy Limited and SEW Energy Limited under the Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) system for 40 years.

However, all opposition parties — NCP, UDP, HSPDP, KHNAM and BJP — had accused the Congress of a total sellout and demanded that the deal be scrapped.

In fact, the NCP and the UDP promised during their Assembly poll campaign that if they are voted to power, the deal will be scrapped.

After forming the Government, the NCP-UDP-led coalition said it would wait for a high-powered committee, led by Chief Secretary Ranjan Chatterjee, to submit its report on the power deal before taking any decision.

The committee recently submitted a 160-page report and it is schedule to be discussed in the Cabinet.

Party workers of UDP and NCP, meanwhile, are demanding that the Government must not renege on its promise and must scrap the deal immediately.

Heading: The importance of being Jyoti Basu - Indian Express
Content:
In what is seen as a move to recruit kids into their ranks, militant outfits in Manipur have been kidnapping school going boys claiming that they had joined their outfits willingly, official sources said here on Monday.

In the second such incident within a week, two schoolboys were reported missing from Thoubal Kiyam Siphai area in Thoubal district, were kidnapped by a militant group on July 8. The boys, A K Ajoy and A K Bipin, both aged 13 were studying in Class VIII, sources said. Parents of both the boys told the local media on Sunday evening that a thorough search for the kids had not yielded results.

Medha, mother of Bipin, said that she received a telephone call on July 9 night from a spokesman of the banned People's Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak (Prepak) General Secretary group, informing her that the boys were in the custody of Prepak.

She said the caller had told her that the boys had joined the outfit 'willingly' but said that her son had gone to a nearby canal for fishing. Both the parents said they had received calls from Prepak General Secretary group telling them not to approach police or the media but said that they had informed the Thoubal police. They were also told that the boys would be 'released' soon.

They said due to threats from the outfit they did not contact the media immediately and appealed to the Prepak General Secretary group to free the boys without harm. Last week, two other boys, YNaobi (13) and Lan Ngamba (11), were kidnapped from Iroisemba in Imphal West district.

Later a spoksman of the militant outfit Prepak Cobra Task Force group told the parents that the boys had 'willingly' joined the Prepak Cobra Task Force group.

Following public protest, Naobi and Ngamba were handed over to Iroisemba Youth Development Club by the militants on July 12, sources said.

Heading: The party can’t afford to hate this rebel - Indian Express
Content:
Looking for solutions to the current political imbroglio, politicians from New Delhi knocked the door of veteran Communist leader, Jyoti Basu, this week.

Barely a few days ago on July 8 as his well-wishers and supporters gathered to greet him on his 95th birthday, Basu had reiterated his wish to work till his last breath.

On July 13, External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee and Lok Sabha Speaker Somnath Chatterjee called on him separately at his Indira Bhavan residence here to seek his opinion on the latest crisis.

With the regimented CPI(M) organisation leaving little scope for anybody, including senior leaders, to speak out against general secretary Prakash Karat, Chatterjee and others know that Basu's status and advice is unmatched, even though the former CM is now a mere permanent invitee to politburo meetings, without any voting power.

Chatterjee, a CPI(M) MP, was miffed by Karat's decision to include his name in the list of MPs sent to the President when the Left decided to withdraw support to the Congress-led UPA Government. Chatterjee wanted to stay on as the Speaker, partly to avoid voting with the BJP against the Congress.

Mukherjee, the Congress leader of the House and the crisis manager, said that he had come to meet Basu since the veteran leader was one of the main architects of the UPA Government.

Whether it is a crisis within the party, or a dispute between the CPI(M) and its Left Front partners, or even a face-off between the state Government and Mamata Banerjee's Trinamool Congress, Basu has always played a critical role in getting people to listen to reason or being an agony aunt. In fact, insiders say that Basu is the only person before whom comrades can unload their grievances.

Basu, known to be a very disciplined leader without any personal axe to grind, is the only senior CPI(M) leader who can make critical statements about the party and get away with it.

Basu's most 'famous' critical statement was made way back in 1996 when Karat and his clique prevented Basu from becoming the PM in a government that could have been formed then with the "outside support" of the Congress. "It was a historic blunder," Basu had said in a detailed interview 10 months later.

Basu opened up a wider debate within the party on whether it should participate in a government with the support of the Congress. But the party could not touch him for embarrassing it publicly.

For the past two years, as the CPI(M) faced the ire of its partners within and Mamata outside over issues like land acquisition for industry, it was Basu who had the last word.

When Mamata was on the warpath over the Singur acquisition and later the Nandigram police firing, she had refused an invitation from Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee to attend an all-party meeting. The CPI(M) then got Basu to talk to her.

Internally, Basu plays a key role too. For example, the party has steadfastly refused to give Subhas Chakraborty any senior post. This year, after the panchayat elections, Basu forced the party to induct him into the state secretariat.

Ailing for years, Basu is nowadays practically confined to his bedroom and avoids attending public programmes. But senior leaders — from Prakash Karat to the CM and CPI(M) state secretary Biman Bose — have called on him several times, whenever they needed a solution to a deadlock.

Harkishen Singh Surjeet, the party's troubleshooter in Delhi, is a year junior to Basu, but in worse health. So, not only has Basu become lonelier as he can rarely meet Surjeet, but he has to also absorb the entire Delhi pressure alone.

Heading: Defamation laws: It’s a question of honour - Indian Express
Content:
Maverick - that's how media describes West Bengal Minister for Sports and Transport Subhas Chakraborty. Controversy stalks the minister, who often gives the party ideology a go-by. Whether it is organising Hope-86 or visiting the Tarapith shrine in September 2006 or opposing the candidature of Prasun Mukherjee for the post of CAB president, one can see him swimming against the tide.

Starting his career as a student leader in Dum Dum Motijheel College in the 1960's, it's his devotion to veteran Communist leader Jyoti Basu that reportedly earned him a berth in the state secretariat on May 26 this year. In fact, Basu had even made a statement before the media that Chakraborty should be included in the central committee. Chakraborty, on his part, paid rich tributes to Basu after his induction into the state secretariat.

Besides being a fund-raiser for his party, Chakraborty is also known to be a man of the masses. Perhaps that's the reason why the party has never taken any action against him — even when he described senior leaders as a cattle herd, ahead of the 2001 Assembly polls. Asked how he puts up with Chakraborty, Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee said: "Subhas has a past."

Recalling the minister's early days in Motijheel College, RSP Councillor from Dum Dum municipality Niranjan Bhattacharya, who was the head clerk of the college in the 1960's, said: "Whenever a student was unable to pay his fees or was in any kind of distress, Subhas used to go out of his way to help that student."

Chakraborty's elder brother Chiraranjan says that the leader is still the first one to help people in distress. "He is very accessible. Even a rickshaw-puller can approach him," he said, adding that their house, Matrichchaya, on Private Road, Dum Dum, is regularly frequented by those who need assistance of any kind.

Chakraborty has bailed out the party on several occasions. In 1993, when the disciples of Balak Bramhachari, chief of a religious sect called Santan Dal, refused to part with the guru's body saying that there would be a resurrection of their master, it was Chakrabarty who mobilised his cadre and with the help of the police recovered the body of the spiritual leader and organised a cremation. Again in 1996, in order to get rid of hawkers on Kolkata's pavements, who were hampering vehicular traffic on the city's roads, he successfully launched Operation Sunshine to solve the problem. During that time he made a statement: "Except bringing a dead man to life, I can do anything." That perhaps aptly describes the minister's zeal and mindset.

Heading: No power for the parched state - Indian Express
Content:
Countries across the world have defamation laws in accordance with their social setup and legal system. Here's a look at defamation laws in various countries:

India

Definition: Defamation may be by words, either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or visible representation. Any person who makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person, knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, to defame that person.

Some defences: Truth published for public interest is the best defence.

•Any expression in good faith on the conduct or character of a public servant on a public question.

•Publication of a substantially true report.

•It is not defamation to prefer in good faith an accusation against any person to any of those who have lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject matter of accusation.

•It is not defamation to make an imputation on the character of another person, provided it is made in good faith by person for protection of his or other's interests.

Punishment: Section 500 of IPC prescribes imprisonment for a term that may extend to two years, or fine, or both.

The US

•The Government introduced the Defamation Bill, 1988. Truth was not a defence under the Bill. This Bill never became a law.

•Defamation law in the United States is much less plaintiff-friendly than its counterparts in European and Commonwealth countries.

•A defamation on the Internet could be contested in any country in which it was read. American law only allows one claim for the primary publication.

•Most defendants in defamation lawsuits are newspapers or publishers, which are involved in about twice as many lawsuits as are television stations. Most plaintiffs are corporations, businessmen, entertainers and other public figures, and people involved in criminal cases.

•Defamation per se: Allegations or imputations injurious to another in their trade, business, or profession, of loathsome disease, of unchastity and of criminal activity.

Ireland

Defamation Act 1961

•Section 19 of the Act defines defamation as "words calculated to damage the complainant's reputation in his "office, profession, calling, trade or business", are actionable without proof of actual damage — even if the words do not refer to the plaintiff's business."

•Section 21: If a person innocently publishes a defamatory statement, he may make an offer of amends. If the offer is accepted and the apology published, the complainant may not sue the publisher for defamation.

•The apology rendered must be sufficient and the publisher must take all reasonably practical steps to inform anyone who received a written copy of the statement that the words were alleged to be defamatory.

Australia•Defamation Act (January 1, 2006) does not include a definition, but is based on the common law approach that defamation concerns injury to reputation by: exposing a person to hatred, contempt or ridicule; or lowering a person's estimation in the eyes of right minded observers; or making others shun or avoid a person.

•The Act introduced an offer-of-amends process aimed at reducing defamation litigation and provide for an extended qualified privilege defence based on public interest and reasonable conduct on the part of the publisher.

•In a jury trial, they would determine whether the publication was defamatory and whether defences succeeded, and judges would determine damages, if any.

Pakistan

•The aim is to counter blasphemy.

•In 1982, President Zia ul-Haq added Section 295B to the Pakistan Penal Code punishing "defiling the Qur'an" with life imprisonment.

•In 1986, Section 295C was introduced, mandating death penalty for use of derogatory remarks for the Prophet.

•In 1990, the Federal Shari'ah Court ruled in favour of mandatory death sentence, with no right to reprieve or pardon. The government is yet to formally amend the law.

•In 2004, the Pakistani Parliament approved a law to reduce the scope of the blasphemy laws. Police officials will have to investigate accusations of blasphemy to ensure that they are well-founded, before presenting criminal charges. 

Source: Legal websites

HIGH-PROFILE DEFAMATION CASES

Although lawsuits are routinely slapped on publications and media houses, the Defamation Act — which covers statements or 'representations' made intentionally even though the person making them knows that they can damage the reputation of the target — has also been invoked against law enforcement, politicians and organisations. Here are some recent defamation suits that made news in India:

July 2008: Even though the CBI has, ostensibly, solved the convoluted Arushi-Hemraj murder case, the courtroom has probably not seen the last of Dr Rajesh Talwar, once the prime accused in the slayings of his daughter, Arushi, and domestic help, Hemraj. Now, the dentist's lawyer, Pravin Rai, has asserted that Talwar plans to file a defamation case against the UP police, which, despite a lack of forensic evidence, accused him of perpetrating the double murders, as a result of which he had to spend about two months in jail.

 

May 2008: Australian entertainer and aspiring Bollywood actress Tania Zaetta demanded an apology from the Australian Government and filed a $1 million defamation lawsuit over rumours that she had sex with Australian soldiers during a goodwill mission in Afghanistan.

 

April 2008: Notices for defamation and libel were served to three members of the Forum for Saving Gandhi's Heritage for taking out a full-page advertisement in the New York Times levelling several accusations against Sonia and Rahul Gandhi during the Congress president's visit to New York. The Indian National Overseas Congress , which filed the lawsuit in the New York Supreme Court, is demanding $100 million in damages for the "intentionally false" statements and for inciting "evil opinions" about the mother-son duo.

 

February 2008: TDP leader N Janardhan Reddy was sentenced to six months in jail and fined Rs 5,000 for maligning the reputation of Rural Development Minister G Chinna Reddy. Accusing the minister of being a "cheat", Janardhan had alleged that Chinna Reddy's doctorate degree was fake.

Heading: Centre calls meet of Naxal-hit states - Indian Express
Content:
For the third time this month, the state Government has announced more power cuts for cities and rural areas. The state-run Central Power Distribution Company of AP Limited has even issued an advisory to consumers to minimise their use of air conditioners, electric cookers etc, and opt for power saving tube lights. A once-a-week power holiday has also been forced upon the industries, as the state reels under frequent and long power cuts.

The scanty rainfall has led to a fall in hydel power generation as well. The Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation Limited (APGENCO) is the third largest power utility in the country in terms of its installed capacity (6760.9 MW). Its hydro installed capacity of 3586.4 MW is the highest in the country. However, the lack of rains has drastically reduced hydel power generation, leading to a crisis that only threatens to worsen as the dry spell continues.

Energy Minister Shabbir Ali Mohammed says that the state is facing a shortage like never before. He says that against a demand of 175 million units, the state is able to procure only 155 million units from all the available sources. With water levels in the reservoirs falling, hydel power generation is only 14 million units against the usual 45 million units, he claims. In June-July 2007, the hydel power generation was 48 million units per day. He says that the scanty rainfall and the extended dry spell have triggered this crisis.

The Met Department says that the situation may continue for some more days and unless cyclonic systems develop over the Bay of Bengal, the state will not receive adequate rainfall.

Energy department officials say that the present shortfall of 1000 MW will increase in the next couple of weeks, as rains have also failed in neighbouring areas due to which there is no fresh inflow in both the main rivers, Godavari and Krishna.

The thermal power plants are working at optimum capacity, generating 69.67 million units to fulfil a portion of the demand. Andhra Pradesh has six thermal power stations and 13 hydro power stations.

The huge gap in demand and supply is taking a heavy toll on the four distribution companies — central, eastern, southern and northern — that have sought drastic measures and have issued advisories to commercial establishments to minimise power consumption, asking them to switch-off neon signboards and decorative lights.

Chief Minister Y S Rajasekhara Reddy reviewed the power situation on Saturday after which officials announced two to three-hour power cuts in municipal corporation areas, four-hour cuts in towns and seven hour-cuts in rural areas, besides a power holiday for industries.

However, the state Government has promised seven hours of uninterrupted power supply to the farm sector as a part of the poll promise. Sources say that to maintain supply to the farm sector the Government has gone for power cuts in cities and towns.

The central grid is also unable to fulfil the state's power requirements, as all southern states are facing similar shortages and drawing power from there. The state is already buying 700 MW power from other states and has been spending Rs 10 crore per day for the last 12 days.

Besides cities and towns, the industry is bearing the brunt of unscheduled power cuts and emergency load-sheddings for the past three weeks. Production has been hit due to the daily power cuts, leading to protests from industry associations. The Federation of Small Industries Associations has suggested that instead of cutting power several times in a day, the Government should declare a weekly power holiday. Mohammed says that the state Government has accepted this proposal and industrial areas will have a power holiday on a rotation basis.

According to sources in the industry, this is the first time that the state faces such an acute power crisis in the last five years.

The state capital will have a power cut of two to three hours daily, while the Central Power Distribution Company Limited has been directed to enforce power holiday once a week in all the industries under its jurisdiction in and around Hyderabad.

Heading: Chhattisgarh to act tough on cops avoiding Bastar posting - Indian Express
Content:
Andhra Pradesh, which has been more effective in dealing with the problem of Naxalites, has been asked by the Centre to share its experiences with other Naxal-affected states, particularly neighbouring Orissa which has been receiving a large of number of Naxalites who are on the run in Andhra.

The Centre has called a meeting of four Naxal-affected states — Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa — on Wednesday to take stock of the situation, Home Ministry sources said on Monday. They said the meetings, which would be chaired by Home Secretary Madhukar Gupta, would take place in two sessions, first with officials of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh and then with those of Orissa and Andhra Pradesh. The states will be represented by their chief secretaries and directors general of police.

The states have been asked to apprise the Centre in detail about the steps they have been taking to contain the Naxal menace. The effectiveness of various developmental programmes, launched by the Centre as well as the states, in these areas will also come up for discussion.

Sources said the Centre was also likely to ask the state governments to improve their coordination and see Naxalism as a threat to the entire country and not just to their respective states. In this regard, Andhra Pradesh will be asked to share its experiences with others. The Naxalites groups in Andhra are said to be under tremendous pressure from the state police and many of them are shifting their operations to other states, particularly Orissa. A number of Naxal activities in Orissa in recent times have been carried out by Naxal groups based in Andhra. These groups strike in Orissa before coming back to their hideouts in Andhra.

Sources said Andhra Pradesh experience, especially the training they have imparted to its police forces in jungle warfare, could prove to be extremely useful for other states. The meeting with Home Secretary is likely to be followed by another meeting of the state Government officers with the Cabinet Secretary on Friday, the sources said. At this meeting, the secretaries and heads of departments of the various developmental units of the state Government were also likely to be present.

Besides other things, the meeting with the Cabinet Secretary is also expected to assess the status of the formation of a central anti-Naxal force that the Prime Minister had promised last year. The proposal to set up this force is likely to be put before the Cabinet anytime now.

The anti-Naxal force is planned to be set up with the personnel of CRPF who will undergo specialised training to fight the Naxalites. In fact, two battalions of CRPF personnel are already undergoing training and would be ready to be deployed in about 2-3 months.

Once the Cabinet gives its approval, eight more battalions of this anti-Naxal force would be raised, the sources said.

Heading: More ITBP jawans could head for Afghanistan - Indian Express
Content:
With the reluctance of police personnel towards posting in Naxalite areas, Chhattisgarh Government is now gearing up to act tough against those who avoid joining duties in the tribal Bastar region.

Police personnel at all levels are averse towards their posting in Naxalite areas, particularly in Dantewada, Bijapur, Narayanpur, Bastar and Kanker districts, which have become a hotbed of Maoist rebels with violence and bloodshed during the last few years.

Immediately after the Police department released the list of transfers this year, Police Establishment Board was flooded with applications of those who were transferred to Bastar, requesting for cancellation or change in place of posting mainly on health grounds and other reasons. Nearly 65 per cent of the inspectors shifted to Bastar region from other districts have requested for change in posting on health grounds and other reasons while about half of the 41 sub-inspectors, including women, have sought cancellation or modification of transfer order, police sources said.

The Police Establishment Board, headed by Director General of Police Vishwaranjan, has examined these requests and took a view against change in transfer orders, except in few genuine cases of women police personnel, who have to look after their kids. Even in such cases, the option considered is to reduce the distance by changing their place of posting from the remote areas of Dantewada and Bijapur to other less sensitive places in Bastar and Kanker districts.

The Board has also refused to consider applications of those police personnel who on previous occasions had managed to get their transfers to Naxalite areas of Bastar cancelled. A number of requests, which came through other routes than proper channel, were not being considered, sources said.

"We have formulated a transfer policy for the Naxalite areas and transfers were done accordingly. Anyone not reporting for duty at their place of posting in Bastar region will face action", said state Home Minister Ramvichar Netam.

However ruling BJP legislator Devji Bhai Patel, who raised the issue of police posting in Naxal areas during the just-concluded monsoon session of Vidhan Sabha , is not convinced. "The rules appears to be applicable only for those in the lower ranks as senior police personnel always manage to get their transfers to Naxalite areas cancelled," he said. A number of head constables, posted in Naxalite areas for five years, could not be shifted out as relievers were not reporting for duty, he added.

Heading: DMK convenes high-level meet to discuss attack on fishermen - Indian Express
Content:
With the recent bombing at the Indian Embassy in Kabul pointing to a heightened threat to Indian installations in Afghanistan, the Government is considering strengthening the presence of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) in that country.

Home Secretary Madhukar Gupta on Monday told reporters that the Government was not averse to increasing the number of ITBP personnel deployed in Afghanistan 'if required'.

As of now, there are about 400 ITBP jawans deployed in various cities of Afghanistan, including Kabul, Kandahar and Jalalabad, to protect Indians working in that country on different projects. The force is also responsible for guarding the Indian Embassy in Kabul and other Indian installations.

The role of the ITBP in safeguarding India's interests has come in for a lot of praise. The force has lost four of its personnel, including two in last week's attack on the embassy, while several have been injured protecting life and property of Indians who have been targeted by a number of terrorist organisations.

Gupta's remark comes in the wake of a two-day visit to Afghanistan by Foreign Secretary Shiv Shanker Menon and other officials, including ITBP ADG Ranjeet Sinha. The Home Secretary said a decision about strengthening the ITBP presence would be taken after discussions with Menon and Sinha about the security situation in Afghanistan.

Sinha, who returned from his second trip to Afghanistan in about a month, said the official delegation had had made a detailed assessment of security requirements for Indian installations in view of the increased and continuing threat to the Indians operating in that country.

He said it was decided to further beef up the security arrangements for the heavily-fortified Indian embassy in Kabul, as well as the residence of the Indian Ambassador who had escaped unhurt in the last week's bombing. Security around India's consulates in Kandahar and Jalalabad were also being tightened, he said.

The Ministry of External Affairs had also decided to purchase and install state-of-the-art security equipment to meet operational requirements of the ITBP.

Only last month, one ITBP jawan was killed and four injured in a suicide bombing near Afganistan-Iran border, about 300 km west of Kabul, where India's Border Roads Organisation is constructing a 210-km Zaranj-Delaram road. The road is extremely important for Afghanistan's strategic interests.

Heading: Sarath says his party favours third front minus DMK, ADMK - Indian Express
Content:
Coming under criticism from almost all political parties in Tamil Nadu for the continuing attack on fishermen, the DMK has convened a meeting of its high-level policy implementation committee on July 17 to discuss the issue.

In the most recent attack on fishermen from the state, allegedly by Sri Lankan Navy, two fishermen from Nagapattinam — Vasagan and Narayanan — were killed while the third — Murali — was injured on Saturday, drawing instant and intense criticism from almost all political parties in the state.

Murali informed his parents about the attack over his cellphone and was rescued by other fishermen from his village, who rushed to the spot on their motorboats.

Both the AIADMK and PMK have demanded that the state Government should take up the issue with the Centre.

In her statement on Sunday, Opposition leader and AIADMK general secretary Jayalalithaa demanded that Tamil Nadu should get an assurance from Sri Lanka that such killings would not take place in the future.

In a similar note, PMK's S Ramadoss asked the state Government to take up the issue with the Prime Minister and External Affairs Minister to stop the frequent attacks.

The CPI has also taken up the issue and would organise a march to the Lankan Deputy High Commission in Chennai to protest against the attacks. Party's state secretary D Pandian has urged the Centre to take up the issue with the Sri Lankan Government during the SAARC conference, to be held in Lanka.

The DMK meeting on July 17 will discuss how to prevent such incidents, said party general secretary and Finance Minister K Anbazhagan in a statement here.

Chief Minister M Karunanidhi had expressed his concerns over the issue publicly and has also written to the Centre to intervene in the problem.

The Lankan Navy on the other hand, has denied any role in the killing of the fishermen, maintaining that it is the handiwork of LTTE cadres.

Heading: IISST gets ‘deemed to be varsity’ status - Indian Express
Content:
Taking on the Goliaths is the political flavour of this season. Days after PMK announced that it was working at a coalition sans the two major political parties in Tamil Nadu, DMK and AIADMK, actor Sarath Kumar, founder of the nascent AISMK, said his party was looking for a third front in the state in the run-up to the next Lok Sabha elections.

Talking to reporters during his 54th birthday celebrations in Chennai on Monday, Sarath said his party was looking to lead an alliance "with parties that share a common vision" without DMK or AIADMK.

"AISMK has identified 22 constituencies where we would field candidates for the coming general elections," he said. This would be the first time the party is taking part in the election after its formation recently.

Fellow actor and DMDK founder Vijayakanth's stated plan is to forge an alliance other than the two major Dravidian parties.

The AISMK is now the third party that is looking to forge a new alliance that can take on both DMK and AIADMK, something that has not been tried successfully so far.

Curiously, the Congress, now part of the DMK alliance, fits in the plans of all three fronts. Vijayakanth had held discussions with AICC in-charge Arun Kumar while PMK founder S Ramadoss went a step further by announcing that it was looking at an alliance led by the Congress.

Sarath Kumar, a member of the Nadar community, was a DMK MP before quitting the party to form his own outfit.

Heading: Report on TN phone tapping row submitted - Indian Express
Content:
The Thiruvanthapuram based Indian Institute of Space Science & Technology (IISST) established in September 2007 has been granted 'deemed to be university' status by the University Grants Commission (UGC).

Set up under the aegis of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), IIST is the world's first space university to offer undergraduate programmes. From this academic year, it will also start three post-graduate programmes in areas of specific interest to the ISRO.

The Department of Space had proposed that IISST be given 'deemed to be university' status. The UGC had given its go-ahead to the proposal in January 2008. The functioning of the IISST and its performance shall now be reviewed annually by the UGC through its Expert Committee. The status of the IISST will be confirmed after five years on the basis of performance reports of the Expert Review Committee of the UGC and the recommendation of the Commission. The IISST, meanwhile will not be permitted to engage in any activities that are commercial in nature.

ISS accounts shall now be open to audit by the CAG of India and there shall also be no diversion of assets of the IISST Society without prior permission of the Government of India or the UGC.

Heading: Patan gangrape victim returns to college with police protection - Indian Express
Content:
After a three-month probe in the phone tapping controversy, a single-member Commission submitted its report to Chief Minister M Karunanidhi on Monday, though the details of it are not known yet.

A seemingly ordinary conversation between Chief Secretary L K Tripathy and Chief Vigilance Commissioner S K Upadhyay was published by an English daily here in April, along with the report that the phones of several leaders were being tapped by the state.

In the recorded conversation, the officials were heard discussing a case related to the Kodanadu Estate owned by Opposition leader J Jayalalithaa.

Some of the numbers that the daily claimed were being tapped included that of PMK founder and staunch DMK baiter S Ramadoss, senior journalists and academicians. Ramadoss took up the issue and had raised the allegation against the state Government several times in the past.

The Government soon formed a committee to find the source of tapping and also that of the leak, entrusting the task on P Shanmugam, a retired justice of the Madras High Court. In the past three months since its formation, the committee summoned several persons including journalists who reported the issue.

In the meanwhile, Janata Party president Subramaniam Swamy came out with a tape that had the conversation between then Social Welfare Minister Dr Poongothai Aladi Aruna and Upadhyay, in which the Minister was heard asking the official to go easy on her relative who was caught in a bribery case.

Admitting that it was indeed her voice, Poongothai tendered resignation after the incident, while the Government forwarded the case to the same commission.

Though the details of the report are not known, it is learnt that the Vigilance office was the source of the leak.

Heading: Doc murder: accused ‘admits’ to killing 5 more on trains - Indian Express
Content:
The victim in the Patan gangrape case returned to her hostel at the Primary Teacher's Certificate (PTC) College on Monday under police protection. "The fast track court has accepted our plea to send her back to normal college life," said Manjula Pradeep of Navasrjan Trust, which had the girl's custody after she left her father's home.

"She will remain under full police protection, both at the hostel and college," she added.

Meanwhile, the court has rejected defence's application demanding separate chargesheets for different accused. The court observed that proceedings will continue with single chargesheet on July 21. It further said that the proceedings will be stopped if the defence counsel gets a stay order from the High Court.

Five accused — Manish Parmar, Ashwin Parmer, Mahendra Prajapati, Atul Patel, and Suresh Patel — have been booked for rape and unlawful compulsory labour. Another teacher, Kiran Patel, who is physically challenged, has been charged with committing 'unnatural offences'.

The girl was allegedly raped 14 times between September 2007 and January 2008 by her teachers.

Heading: Ex-CJI backed Indira Govt in Emergency case - Indian Express
Content:
In his narco-analysis test, prime accused in the murder of Kanpur-based gastroenterologist Dr Anurag Mittal has reportedly confessed to five more murders.

The accused, Brijesh Kumar Verma, a resident of Unnao, had reportedly confessed to have killed the doctor on board Shram Shakti Express on August 28. In his confession, he listed the trains on which he carried out the five murders. He gave the details of the places where he threw the bodies of the victim. Verma, however, was unaware of the name of the victims.

Investigating officer, Inspector Dileep Kumar Mittal of Government Railway Police (GRP), Aligarh Cantonment, said he has sent the report to his seniors and also to the districts where Verma said he had thrown the bodies.

According to Dileep Kumar, the trains on which Verma claimed to have committed murders are Kanyakumari Express, Kalka Mail and Amritsar Express. Verma threw the bodies out of the train so that the crimes looked like accidents.

According to the postmortem report, Dr Mittal was strangled to death. The doctor was reportedly carrying Rs 1 lakh, US $ 8,000 and other valuables which were found missing. Failing to solve the case, the government handed over the case to the Special Task Force (STF) from the GRP.

During the investigation, the police found that Dr Mittal's cell phone was still in use. The STF also came to know that one B K Singh was travelling in the same coach along with Dr Mittal. From the railway record, they found that Singh was a resident of Rajajipuram in Lucknow, but did not find him in the same address.

Working on these clues, STF arrested Verma from Chowk area of Lucknow on September 1. It recovered two mobile phones, including the one belonging to Dr Mittal, and US $ 8,000 dollars, looted from Dr Mittal.

Even after Verma's arrest, there were several unanswered questions, said Kumar. "It was not clear how he came to know that Dr Mittal was carrying a large amount of money. Why did he kill the doctor and who else were with him?" said Dileep Kumar.

The police, therefore, obtained permission from the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate of Aligarh for the narco-analysis test.

Heading: In Pune, malls to be manned by SC/ST youths - Indian Express
Content:
Former Chief Justice of India Yeshwant Vishnu Chandrachud, who passed away at Bombay Hospital after battling cardiac ailments for long, was remembered today as a stalwart of judiciary.

Elevated to the Supreme Court in August 1972, he became the Chief Justice in February 1978 and retired seven years later, becoming the longest-serving judge in the apex court and CJI. During his tenure, he passed several landmark judgments, the foremost being as part of the majority bench that decided in favour of the Indira Gandhi government in a habeas corpus case during the Emergency.

In one of the most notable cases in Indian Constitutional history, Chandrachud was on the Bench comprising five most senior judges that heard a case related to whether the right to habeas corpus (Article 21 of the Constitution) could be suspended during periods of national emergency after petitions were moved by scores of MISA detenues.

Despite widespread high court support for habeas corpus, Justice Chandrachud went along with Justices A N Ray, P N Bhagawati and M H Beg in a 4-1 verdict to reject the petitions on April 28, 1976. The judges held that no person has any locus to move any writ petition under Article 226 before a high court for habeas corpus or any other writ to challenge the legality of an order of detention.

The only dissenting opinion was from Justice H R Khanna, who has been widely acclaimed for the act.

A diehard cricket fan, Chandrachud was also appointed by the Indian cricket board to probe allegations of betting and match-fixing in Indian cricket that had rocked the sport in the nineties. He gave a clean chit to the Indian players in April 2000.

Noting that "we know him (Chandrachud) through his judgments", Additional Solicitor General Rajendra Raghuvanshi regretted on Monday that they had not had the privilege of knowing the judge in those days. "He was a stalwart of judiciary, a prominent educationist who devoted time for legal education after he retired."

Born in Pune on July 12, 1920, Chandrachud came to Mumbai for his graduation from Elphinstone College, majoring in History and Economics. He did his Law from Law College at Pune, and enrolled as an advocate, practising at the Bombay High Court, in 1943.

From 1952 to 1958, Chandrachud served as government pleader and was appointed as a judge of the Bombay High Court in March 1961.

He headed the one-man pay commission for fixing pay scales of Bombay Municipal Corporation Officers and was arbitrator in the dispute between the Bombay Electrical Supply and Transport Undertaking and the BEST Employees' Union.

The historical inquiry into the circumstances leading to the death of Jan Sangh leader Deen Dayal Upadhyaya was also conducted by him as a one-man commission.

"We have lost a great judge who had a foresight in law. His biggest judgment was when he defined what cruelty is and included mental cruelty in the Hindu Marriage Act when he was a Supreme Court judge," said V G Palshikar, former acting chief justice of the Bombay High Court.

"He was a legend in his own time and one of the greatest judges SC has produced," said V A Gangal, former president of the Advocates Association of Western India.

Expressing deep sorrow at Chandrachud's death, Maharashtra Governor S C Jamir said: "With his passing away, the chapter of the old legal luminaries has come to a close. But he has left behind a legacy which will continue to inspire the new generation in the country." In his condolence statement, Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh said the country has lost a senior legal luminary.

Heading: 32 Indians on way to Pope function go missing in New Zealand - Indian Express
Content:
A mall may be as far as it gets from a village, but here in Pune, the symbol of urbanisation is providing an answer to rural unemployment.

In a unique initiative, 286 Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe youth have been placed in various malls in the city since January this year, after a 45-day training course undertaken by the district employment agency.

In all, 360 rural youth undertook the training course to be groomed as sales staff for retail stores, including auto shops. All of them were in the 18-25 age group, and none had cleared Class X.

The initiative follows a resolution passed by the Maharashtra government to place rural youth from reserved categories in malls as sales staff. Pune has taken the lead, and Mumbai and Nagpur will follow suit.

"The government has sponsored the programme and is spending Rs 5,000 per applicant on training," says G A Sangde, the Assistant Director of the employment agency.

"From bookstores such as Landmark and Crossword to malls such as SGS and Pune Central and even big retail outlets in the city, the training has ensured them placement. We will also be trying to place the rest," says Anil Deshmukh, Director, MARKS (Management and Retail Knowledge Solutions), who conducted the training on behalf of the employment exchange. "We have 58 outlets on our list and, as and when the demand arises, they contact us," he adds.

Under the training, held in several batches, the youth were taught communication skills and personality and retail management for a month and a half, apart from credit card management as well as customer service. A mall visit is also part of the course.

The process is fairly simple. "Once they apply, the youth are told about the training and if they have an interest in retail management are suggested to go for training at three centres in the city run by different agencies who have assured placement. The scheme is mainly for the economically backward and for the reserved categories," explains Sangde.

Deshmukh says there is enough demand and the youth they had trained had got placement. "Our task is to remove their apprehensions and make them confident. They are doing well now," he said.

The 286 youth have started with a salary of Rs 4,000-Rs 5,000, Deshmukh says, and they expect some to get promoted as floor managers.

Shilpa Shinde, who works with My Dollar Store on Bhandarkar Road, is full of confidence. "The course has helped us a lot. I am able to handle the retail segment with ease," she says.

Heading: Orissa to rethink subsidised rice for APL families - Indian Express
Content:
As many as 32 Indian Catholic pilgrims are understood to have gone missing during a stopover on their way to Australia for World Youth Day according to New Zealand immig-ration officials.

The pilgrims have gone missing over the past four or five days, the Agence France Presse has said, citing a statement issued by the Immigration Department.

The officials said that the Department of Labour is working with the Catholic Church in New Zealand to look for the pilgrims, who went missing soon after arriving last week en route to Sydney, where Pope Benedict XVI will lead World Youth Day celebrations later this week.

When contacted, Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs officials said that they were communicating with the embassies in Australia and New Zealand to get more details.

A total of 220 Indian Catholics were given one-month visitor visas for New Zealand, and they were due to leave for Australia tomorrow.

While they have the legal right to remain in New Zealand until their visas expire, immigration officials say they want to ensure that the pilgrims continue their trip to Australia as previously arranged.

New Zealand Catholic Church spokeswoman Lyndsay Freer said the pilgrims arrived early last week in New Zealand, where they were met by local Catholic parish representatives. "The rest went to the various homes they were to be billeted at, and after a day or so kind of disappeared. In terms of the law it's not illegal, but it's certainly most extraordinary and most disappointing," she said.

More than 100,000 foreign pilgrims are expected in Sydney for this week's celebrations which begin Tuesday and end with a papal mass on Sunday.
